tales.title: I saw the schooner come in
text: When a schooner comes in, all the boys in town run down to the river mouth to watch. You can see her from far out, her sails like a white bird on the lake, and then she comes in between the piers, and the sailors throw ropes, and the men on the wharf pull her in.

I want to be a sailor. My father says sailors drown, and drink, and never come home. I do not care. Last week a sailor let me climb up the rigging to the first crosspiece and look out over the whole town. You could see everything, all the roofs and the fort and the prairie going on forever. I am going to be a sailor. Do not tell my father.

tales.title: I lost my boot
text: Yesterday I was walking to school on Clark Street and I stepped in the mud and my foot went in up to the knee. When I pulled it out, my boot stayed in. I could see the top of it, but I could not reach it, and every time I tried I sank deeper.

A man came by with a board and laid it across the mud and fished my boot out with a stick. He said that was the third boot he had rescued that week. He said one day he is going to open a shop selling boots that people lost in the mud. I went to school with one muddy boot. The teacher made me sit by the door.

tales.title: The Indian boy and the bow
text: There is a Potawatomi boy who comes into town with his father to trade, and he can shoot a bird out of the air with a little bow. He showed me how. You hold it like this, and pull back to your ear, and let go smooth, not jerky. I tried and the arrow went straight into the ground.

He laughed so hard he fell over. Then he gave me the bow. I gave him my best marble, the blue one. My mother says his people are going away soon, far west across the big river. I asked him about it with my hands and he nodded and pointed at the sun going down. I am keeping the bow forever.

tales.title: I heard a wolf
text: Last winter, on a very cold night, I woke up and heard a wolf howling, out on the prairie past our house. It went up and up and then down, and then another one answered, and another, until there were lots of them all singing together.

I got into my sister's bed and we pulled the quilt over our heads. In the morning my father showed us the tracks in the snow, right up to our pig pen. The pigs were all fine. My father said the wolves were only singing to the moon. I asked him what the moon sang back. He did not know.

tales.title: School in a church
text: I go to school in the back of the Baptist church, with thirty other children on long benches. We have slates and one book for every three children. The teacher has a long stick and she can reach anybody on any bench without getting up.

There is a French girl who speaks no English, and an Irish boy who speaks it so fast nobody understands him, and twin girls from Vermont who say they are going to be teachers too. I am going to be a lawyer, like my father. Or a sailor. I have not decided. The teacher says I should decide to learn my letters first.

tales.title: Mr. Beaubien's fiddle
text: Mr. Beaubien at the Sauganash has more children than anybody in Chicago, and they are all my friends. On Saturday nights we sit on the stairs and watch the grown-ups dance, and Mr. Beaubien plays the fiddle and stamps his foot and sings in French, and everybody spins round and round until they fall over.

He saw me on the stairs once and winked and played a tune just for me, a fast one, and all the grown-ups had to dance faster. Go and find him. If you are a child he will give you a piece of sugar. If you are a grown-up he will make you dance.

tales.title: The fort's drum
text: Every morning the drum at the fort wakes up the soldiers, and it wakes me up too, because our house is near the fort. Rat-a-tat-tat. Then the fife. Then the soldiers shout.

I sneak over to watch them drill sometimes. They march up and down and turn all together, and the sergeant shouts things nobody can understand, and a little boy my age beats the drum. He is a drummer boy. I asked him how you get to be a drummer boy and he said you have to run away from home. I am thinking about it.

tales.title: Skating on the river
text: In the winter the river froze so hard you could drive a wagon across it. Everybody went skating, grown-ups and children, up and down the river from the fort to the forks. My brother made me skates from old knife blades bound to wooden soles with leather.

I fell down a hundred times. Then I did not fall down. Then I could go fast, faster than my brother. He said it was because I am lighter. I said it was because I am better. We had a race to the forks and I won. He says I cheated. I did not cheat. I am just faster.

tales.title: Strawberries on the prairie
text: In June the prairie is covered with wild strawberries, little red ones hidden in the grass, sweeter than any garden strawberry. My mother sends us out with baskets and we come back with red mouths and red hands and half a basket.

You have to watch for snakes. My friend saw a rattlesnake once, coiled up in the grass, shaking its tail like a baby's rattle. We ran all the way home. My mother said that was why we only brought back half a basket. It was not why. But we let her think so.

tales.title: Our new house
text: We used to live in one room behind my father's store, all six of us. Now my father has built a real house, with two rooms downstairs and two upstairs and a real glass window in the front. I have to share a bed with only one sister now instead of two.

It took my father and two carpenters six days to build it. They nailed it together out of thin boards, very fast, and my grandfather, who came from Connecticut, said it would blow away in the first storm. It did not. The storm came and the house just creaked a bit. My grandfather said it was a miracle.

tales.title: The steamboat's whistle
text: The first time I heard a steamboat whistle, I thought it was a monster. It came from out on the lake, a long scream, and then black smoke, and then the boat came in, bigger than the fort, with wheels on its sides going round and round, splashing.

My father lifted me up on his shoulders to see it. People came off it all day, more people than I had ever seen. Now I am not afraid of steamboats. I know every one by its whistle. That one is the Michigan, she has a deep one. I want to be a steamboat captain. Or a sailor. Or a lawyer.

tales.title: When I had the shakes
text: I had the ague all last August. Every afternoon at two o'clock I shook so hard the bed rattled, and my teeth went chatter chatter chatter, and I was so cold even with three quilts. Then I got hot and my mother put wet cloths on my head.

Every morning I felt fine, and I went out to play, and then at two o'clock I had to come home and shake. The doctor gave me quinine, which is so bitter it makes you cry. My mother mixed it with molasses and it was still bitter. In September it went away. My mother says everybody gets it. I hope I never get it again.

tales.title: My name in the newspaper
text: My father's name was in the newspaper last week, in the list of letters waiting at the post office. He did not even know there was a letter. My mother read the list out loud at breakfast, and there it was.

He went to Mr. Hogan's store and paid a whole quarter dollar and got the letter. It was from my grandmother, and it said she was coming to live with us next spring. My father read it twice and went very quiet. My mother laughed and laughed. I like my grandmother. She brings peppermints.

tales.title: The camp by the river
text: Every summer Potawatomi families camp on the edge of town near the river, in houses made of mats and bark. The women sell baskets and berries and maple sugar, and the men sell venison and fish. My mother buys from them.

I used to be scared of them. Then a girl from the camp showed me how to make a doll out of corn husks, with a little husk dress and husk hair. Now we play together when they come. This summer she told me with her hands that they are going far away and will not come back. I made her a doll out of rags with button eyes, to take with her. She gave me a husk one. I sleep with it.

tales.title: The printer's devil
text: I am the printer's devil at the newspaper, which means I do every dirty job there is. I sweep the floor and ink the type and fetch the water and run the papers round town. My hands are black from Monday to Sunday.

But I can read faster than anybody in Chicago, because I read every word of the paper before anybody else does, backwards, while I am setting it. I know all the news first. I know who has died and who is getting married and whose lot has been sold. When I am grown I am going to own a newspaper. I am going to call it something better than the Democrat.

tales.title: Walking out on Sunday
text: There are four young men in Chicago for every young lady, so the young ladies can be very particular. I have been walking out on Sunday afternoons with a carpenter's apprentice, and also with a clerk from Lake Street, and also, once, with a lieutenant from the fort.

My mother says I must choose. My father says I must not choose a lieutenant, because the army will take him off to some fort at the end of the world. My aunt says I must choose the clerk, because clerks become merchants. I am going to choose the carpenter. He makes me laugh, and he built my mother a cupboard for nothing. That is better than the end of the world.

tales.title: I bought a lot
text: I am sixteen and I own a lot on the North Side. I saved my wages from the store for a year, forty dollars, and a land agent sold it to me on credit for two hundred, forty down and the rest when I sell. He says it will be worth five hundred by Christmas.

I have walked out to see it twice. It is a swamp with a dead tree in the middle. But everybody's lot is a swamp with a dead tree in the middle. That is what Chicago is. When the canal comes, the agent says, the swamp will be the middle of a great city. I believe him. I have to. I have forty dollars in it.

tales.title: I ran away to Chicago
text: I ran away from my uncle's farm in New York state when I was fifteen. He beat me and worked me like a horse. I walked to Buffalo and worked my passage on a schooner, scrubbing decks and hauling ropes, and the captain put me ashore at Chicago with a dollar in my pocket.

That was last year. Now I drive a dray for a merchant, and I have a bed in his warehouse, and I eat at his table. Nobody here asks where you came from. Nobody cares. If you can work, you can eat. I have written to my mother to tell her I am alive. I have not told her where I am, in case my uncle comes looking.

tales.title: I want to be a teacher
text: I am fourteen and I help at the little school, minding the youngest ones and hearing their letters. The teacher says I have a gift for it. When I am eighteen she says I could have a school of my own, in one of the new towns going up on the prairie.

My mother wants me to marry. My father wants me to help in the store. I want to teach. There are so many children coming into this country, and so few teachers. A girl can do that. A girl can go out to a new town and be somebody. I would like to be somebody.

tales.title: Carrying water
text: I carry water for my mother's laundry, two buckets on a yoke from the lake, fifteen trips a day. I am fourteen. My father died on the boat coming over, in the fever, and they put him over the side in a sheet. My mother and me and my sisters came on alone.

Now I carry water and run errands for the stores, and my mother washes, and we have a room of our own. On Sundays I go to Mass and then I go down to the river and watch the schooners. One day I am going to be on one of them, going back east, with money in my pocket, to show the old country what a Chicago man looks like.

tales.title: The mud
text: There is mud outside. Lots and lots. It goes squish. I jumped in it.
My mother said oh no. My dress is all brown now. My shoes are gone. My mother says the mud ate them. I think the mud is hungry. Do not jump in the mud.

tales.title: The big boat
text: A big boat came. It had white sails. It was bigger than our house. Everybody ran to see.
My father put me on his shoulders. I could see everything. The men on the boat waved. I waved. When I am big I am going on the boat.

tales.title: Kitty
text: We have a kitty. She is grey. She sleeps by the stove. She is soft.
I pulled her tail. She scratched me. Here, look. It is a red line. My mother kissed it. Now it is better. I do not pull the kitty's tail any more. Not very much.

tales.title: Boom, boom
text: At the fort there is a drum. Boom, boom, boom. It wakes me up. Then the soldiers march.
I have a drum too. It is a pot. I hit it with a spoon. Boom, boom. My mother says not inside. So I go outside and march, like the soldiers. Boom, boom.

tales.title: My sister
text: My sister is big. She is six. She knows all her letters. She can carry the water.
She carries me too, when my legs are tired. She tells me stories at night. When she is gone I cry. Then she comes back. She always comes back.

tales.title: The snow
text: Once there was snow, all white, everywhere. It was so cold. My nose was red.
My brother made a snow man. It had a stick nose. I hugged it and it was cold. Then the sun came and the snow man went away. Where did he go? Nobody knows.

tales.title: The horse
text: There is a horse that pulls the wagon. He is very big. His feet go clop, clop.
The man let me sit on the horse. Up high. I held on to his hair. The horse did not mind. He is a good horse. I gave him some grass. He ate it all up.

tales.title: Sugar
text: At the store there is sugar. It is brown and sweet. The man gave me a little piece.
I ate it fast. Then I wanted more. The man laughed. He said come back tomorrow. I will come back tomorrow. I will come back every day.

tales.title: Nothing to fight
text: I joined the army to see a war. They sent me to Chicago, where the last war was twenty-three years ago and the next one is nowhere in sight. We drill in the morning, we mend the pickets in the afternoon, we stand guard at night, and in between we watch the town grow.

The town is more interesting than the fort. Every day there are new buildings, new people, new taverns. On our day off we go into Lake Street and spend a month's pay in an afternoon. The sergeant says the town is a worse enemy than the Indians ever were. He may be right.

tales.title: The old fort's bones
text: This fort was built in 1816, after the first one was burned in the war. They built it on the same ground, with the same plan, the old men say. Two blockhouses, a palisade, barracks, a magazine. Some of the logs in the stable are supposed to be from the first fort, though nobody can prove it.

When I am on night watch in the south-east blockhouse I look down the shore toward where the massacre was. There is nothing there now but sand and grass. But the old French settlers say that when the wind is right, you can hear the drum. I have never heard it. I do not walk down there at night, all the same.

tales.title: Why men desert
text: Every month a man or two deserts. It is too easy. The town is right there, with its taverns and its land agents, and a man who can carry a hod or drive a team can earn more in a week in Chicago than the army pays him in a month.

So a fellow goes out on pass and does not come back, and the next we hear he is digging foundations on Lake Street under another name, or he has gone west with the wagons. The officers send out a sergeant and a corporal to find him, and they come back with nothing and a sore head from the Sauganash. I will not desert. But I understand the ones who do.

tales.title: The Irish in the ranks
text: Half the company is Irish. We came over to New York with nothing, and the recruiting sergeant found us on the docks and offered us food and a coat and five dollars a month to go and see the West. Many of us took it.

The Yankee soldiers call us Paddies and mock our Mass. The Irish soldiers call them psalm-singers and steal their tobacco. But when it comes to a fight in a tavern, the company stands together, Paddies and psalm-singers both, against the whole town. That is the army. You can hate a man in the morning and fight for him at night.

tales.title: The cholera graves
text: Three years ago, in the Black Hawk war, General Scott's men came here by steamboat with the cholera on board. The fort became a hospital. Men died so fast they buried them in trenches on the lake shore, without coffins, in the night.

I was not here then. But the old sergeant was, and he showed me where the graves are, near the lake below the fort. He says when the lake is high it washes the sand away and bones come up. He says he has reburied more than one. He does not like to talk about it. He drinks a little more than he should. I do not blame him.

tales.title: The lighthouse
text: Beside the fort stands the lighthouse, a tall stone tower with a lamp at the top that the keeper lights every night for the boats on the lake. The first one fell down before it was finished, they say, because the builders were in a hurry. This one was built properly.

On a dark night, from the top of the blockhouse, you can see the lamp throwing its light out over the water, and sometimes far out a little point of light from a schooner coming in. It is a lonely sight. It makes you think about all the people out on that black water, trusting that little flame to bring them home.

tales.title: The major
text: Major Greene commands the fort now. He is a careful officer, an old soldier who has seen a lot of posts, and he does not like this one much. Too close to town, he says. Too many taverns. Too many land speculators trying to buy the fort out from under him.

He has the men drill twice a day so they will not have time to go into town. It does not work. But he is fair, and he does not flog a man for nothing, and when a soldier is sick he sends him to the doctor and not to the guardhouse. Go and see him if you like. He will probably ask you if you want to buy any land. He is joking. Probably.

tales.title: Guarding the payment
text: When the Potawatomi come in for their treaty payment, the soldiers guard the money. Two years ago at the great treaty there were thousands of them camped all round the town, and every trader in the Northwest came to collect what they said they were owed, and every whiskey seller came to take the rest.

We were told to keep order. You cannot keep order in a crowd of eight thousand people with forty soldiers. We kept the money safe, that is all. The rest of it, the whiskey and the fighting and the traders cheating, we watched. They say the people will come in again this year, for the last time, before they go west. I do not want to watch it again.

tales.title: Building the piers
text: The government is building piers out into the lake from the mouth of the river, so the channel will stay open and the sand will not close it again. Lieutenant Allen has had the charge of the works. Great cribs of timber, filled with stone, sunk one by one into the lake.

Some of the soldiers have been hired out to work on it, for extra pay. It is cold, wet, back-breaking work, standing in the lake up to your waist, but it pays. The lieutenant knows every timber and every stone. Go and find him. He will explain how the current carries the sand, and you will wish he had not.

tales.title: The fort's garden
text: Every fort has a garden, and ours is the best in Chicago. Cabbages, turnips, potatoes, onions, beans, peas, corn. We grow enough to feed the garrison all winter, and then some, and the officers sell the rest to the town at a good price.

I was a farmer's son in Ohio, and I joined the army to get away from farming. Now I spend half my time hoeing cabbages. My father would laugh until he was sick. But I will tell you a secret: I like it. A man in a garden in the evening, with the lake behind him and the corn coming up, does not need much more.

tales.title: The fiddler of the company
text: There is a private in our company who plays the fiddle, and on Saturday nights he goes down to the Sauganash and plays with Mark Beaubien. Between the two of them they can keep a room dancing until three in the morning. Mark plays fast and loud and the private plays sweet and slow, and somehow it works.

The officers do not approve. A soldier should not play for money in a tavern. But they come down themselves to dance, so they do not say much. Go and find Mark Beaubien. Ask him which of them is the better fiddler. He will say himself. He is wrong.

tales.title: When the paymaster comes
text: The paymaster comes every two months, if the roads are good, and every four months if they are not. When he comes, every soldier in the fort has his whole pay in his hand at once, and by the next morning half of them have none of it left.

The tavern keepers know when the paymaster is coming before we do. They lay in extra whiskey. The land agents come too, and sell lots to privates who have never owned anything bigger than a knapsack. I bought a lot once. It was under water. I still own it. One day, the agent says, it will be worth a fortune.

tales.title: A coat in summer
text: In July our coats are torture. Heavy blue wool, buttoned to the neck, with the collar up under your chin, and the sun beating down on the parade ground. Men faint at drill. The sergeant lets us unbutton the collar if the major is not looking.

In winter the same coat is not warm enough. The wind off the lake comes through it like it was made of cheese cloth. We wrap ourselves in blankets on guard and stamp our feet. Someone in Washington chose this coat. I would like to meet him. I would like to give him a month on the north-east blockhouse in January.

tales.title: Twenty years in the army
text: I have been a soldier for twenty years. I was a drummer boy in the last war with England, at Lundy's Lane, where I was so frightened I beat the wrong call and nobody noticed because everybody was too busy dying. I have served in Detroit, Green Bay, Fort Snelling, St. Louis. Now Chicago.

Every post is the same and every one is different. Detroit had the French. Green Bay had the snow. Fort Snelling had the Sioux. Chicago has the land agents. I will tell you which is the worst. The land agents. The Sioux at least tell you what they want.

tales.title: Cards in the barracks
text: In the evening, when the drum beats tattoo and we are in barracks, we play cards. Euchre, mostly, and sometimes poker, for tobacco or for buttons, since gambling for money is forbidden. A good player can win a whole button collection in a week.

The champion of the company is a corporal from Kentucky who can remember every card that has been played. Some say he marks them. Nobody can prove it. He has more buttons than anyone else in the army. When he gets out, he says, he is going to sell them all and buy a farm. I think he is joking. With that man, you never know.

tales.title: Watching them go
text: There is a Potawatomi man who comes to the fort gate every few days to sell venison. He is older than me, with grey in his hair, and he speaks a little English and I speak a few words of his language, and we have got to be friends of a kind.

Last week he told me that his people must go west across the Mississippi, by the treaty, within three years, and that most of them will go soon. He said it very calmly, as if he were talking about the weather. Then he said: you soldiers will go too, one day. Your fort will be empty, like ours. I did not know what to say to him.

tales.title: A night in the guardhouse
text: I spent last night in the guardhouse. I came back from town an hour after tattoo, singing, with a goose under my arm that I swear I bought honestly. The sergeant did not believe me about the goose.

The guardhouse is a log room with one window and a bench, and there were three of us in it, all for the same reason. We sang until dawn. The goose sang with us. In the morning the major looked at the three of us and the goose, and sighed, and gave us extra guard duty for a week. The goose he kept. I think he ate it.

tales.title: The sergeant's advice
text: My sergeant has been in the army since before I was born, and he gives the same advice to every recruit. Keep your musket clean, your mouth shut, and your money in your boot. Never volunteer. Never lend money to an officer. Never buy land from a man in a tavern.

I have followed all of it except the last one. He told me I was a fool. I told him the lot would be worth a fortune. He said: son, every lot in Chicago is going to be worth a fortune, and that is exactly why none of them will be. I did not understand him. I think I am starting to.

tales.title: An officer in a speculator's town
text: An officer at this post is a gentleman of some consequence in town. We are invited to every dinner and every dance. Every merchant wants our custom and every land agent wants our money.

I have been offered more lots than there are stars, on easier terms than a bank would give. Half my brother officers have bought. Some have doubled their money already. I have not bought anything. The army moves us every year or two, and I do not want to be at some post on the Arkansas when my lot turns into a fortune, or a lake. My colleagues call me a coward. I call myself a soldier.

tales.title: The treaty of 1833
text: I was here for the great treaty two years ago. Eight thousand Potawatomi and Ottawa and Chippewa camped on the prairie around the town, and for two weeks the government's commissioners sat with the chiefs in a great open tent and bargained for every acre they had left in Illinois.

In the end the chiefs signed. Five million acres, for money and goods and land across the Mississippi. The traders took a great part of the money to pay what they said they were owed. I have seen a great many things in the army. I have never seen so much grief and so much greed in one place at once. This February the Senate ratified it.

tales.title: The last summer here
text: This is the last summer my family will spend at Chicago. By the treaty our chiefs signed two years ago, all our land in this country is sold, and we must go west across the great river within three years. Some families have gone already. We will go soon.

I was born on the Des Plaines. My father is buried there, and his father. I will not see their graves again. The Americans say the new land is good, better than here. Maybe it is. A man does not love land because it is good. He loves it because his people are in it. You cannot carry that in a wagon.

tales.title: The treaty tent
text: Two years ago in the fall, thousands of us came to Chicago for the great council. The commissioners from Washington sat in an open tent and our chiefs sat across from them, and they talked for two weeks. Every trader in the country came, and every whiskey seller, and the town was full of people from one end to the other.

The young men drank and the old men argued and in the end the chiefs signed. Some of them said it was the best they could get, because if they did not sign the Americans would take it anyway. Some of them said they had been tricked. I think both are true. That is the worst kind of treaty: the kind where everyone is right and everyone loses.

tales.title: What the traders took
text: The money for our land was supposed to come to us. Much of it went to the traders instead, to pay what they said we owed them. Every trader in the Northwest came with a paper saying such and such a chief owed him so many hundreds of dollars for goods given on credit.

Some of the debts were true. Some were not. Nobody could tell the difference, and the commissioners did not try very hard. So the traders were paid first and we were paid what was left. I do not hate the traders. Some of them are our friends and our family. But I know who came out of that tent rich, and it was not us.

tales.title: The whiskey sellers
text: When we come into Chicago to trade now, the whiskey sellers are waiting at the edge of town. They sell from the back of a wagon or from a shanty by the river, and they do not care if a man is a chief or a boy. They take furs, blankets, guns, horses, anything.

I have seen men of my own family trade away everything they had for a few days of drinking, and then sit in the mud with nothing. The Americans say this is why we must go west: to get away from the whiskey. But the whiskey will follow us west. It always does. It goes wherever there is something left to take.

tales.title: The chief with the reservation
text: Alexander Robinson, Che-che-pin-qua, is a chief now of the united bands, though his father was a Scotsman. By the treaties he has a reservation on the Des Plaines, two sections of land that are his own, and he will not have to go west if he does not want to.

Some of our people say he has done well for himself. Some say he has done well for himself at our expense. He keeps a house where travellers can stay, and he speaks for us to the Americans. Go and find him. Ask him what will happen to the people when they are gone. He will tell you the truth. That is why some people do not like him.

tales.title: The Englishman
text: Billy Caldwell, whom we call Sauganash, the Englishman, is our voice now with the Americans. His father was an Irish officer of the King. He fought with Tecumseh in the old war and he signed the treaty two years ago, and they say he will go west with the people when the time comes.

He is a hard man to read. He dresses like an American gentleman and speaks like one, and then he sits in council with the chiefs and speaks our language as well as any of them. Go and find him. He has seen everything that has happened to us in the last thirty years, from both sides. Ask him which side he is on. Watch how long it takes him to answer.

tales.title: The game is gone
text: When my father was young there were deer everywhere along the Des Plaines and elk on the prairie. Now there are farms. The deer are few and wild and the elk are gone. A man cannot feed his family by hunting here any more. He must buy flour from the stores like an American.

I have tried farming. My corn is as good as any Yankee's. But the land I farm is not mine any more, by the treaty. Next year a man from Ohio will come with a paper and tell me to get off it. I will not wait for him. I will go before he comes. A man should leave his field with his head up.

tales.title: My son learned to read
text: My son went to the mission school at Carey on the St. Joseph River for two winters, and he can read and write English now, better than some of the Americans in this town. He reads the newspaper to me. He reads me the notices of land for sale. He reads me the treaty.

I do not know if it was right to send him. He came back with short hair and a Bible and the Americans' songs. But he can read their papers, and they cannot fool him. In the west, he says, he will be a clerk for the agent, or an interpreter. Our people will need men who can read. That is what the old world has come to.

tales.title: An old man's words at the council
text: At the great council two years ago, one of our old men stood up and said to the commissioners: our fathers came to this country before yours, and our fathers' graves are here. You want us to go to a country we have never seen, among people we do not know. How would you feel, if we asked you to go?

The commissioner said the President was a father to all of us, and wanted only what was best. The old man said: then let the President come and live among us, and see what is best. Everybody laughed, Americans too. Then they went on with the treaty as if nothing had been said. That is how it always goes.

tales.title: Getting ready to go
text: I am getting my horses ready for the journey west. It is a long way, they say, across Illinois and the great river and into the country beyond, many weeks on the road. The government says it will give us food and wagons. Some of us remember what the government has said before.

So I am drying meat and corn, and mending the saddles, and trading for a good kettle and a second blanket for each of my children. I want to be ready for anything. A man who trusts the government's wagons, my uncle says, will walk west with nothing in his hands.

tales.title: I remember when this was ours
text: I came to Chicago as a boy, when there was the old fort and a few French houses and the Kinzie place, and we were the only people for a hundred miles. We camped by the river every summer, and the traders came to us. Now we come to the town, and stand in the mud on Lake Street, and the Americans walk past us without looking.

Yesterday a man in a fine coat stepped around me on the sidewalk as if I were a puddle. I wanted to say: I was here before your sidewalk. Before your street. Before your town. I did not say it. What would be the use? He would only have walked faster.

tales.title: The chief who saved the settlers
text: In the Black Hawk war three years ago, the Potawatomi chief Shabbona rode through the night to warn the American settlers that Black Hawk's warriors were coming. He saved many lives. The Americans called him a hero.

But Black Hawk's people called him a traitor, and some of our own young men did too. Shabbona says he did what was right. I believe him. But I have noticed that the Americans' gratitude has not saved the rest of us from going west. A man can save a hundred Americans and still lose his country.

tales.title: Selling baskets in town
text: I come into town twice a week with baskets I make from ash splints and sweet grass, and I sell them to the American women at their doors. They pay me in flour or salt or sometimes money. One lady on the North Side always buys two and gives me coffee in her kitchen.

She asked me with her hands where my people would go. I pointed west and made a long road with my fingers. She cried. I did not cry. I have done my crying. I gave her a little basket for her baby, a gift, and went out. I will miss her coffee. I will not miss the mud.

tales.title: My mother's grave
text: My mother is buried on a little rise by the Des Plaines, under an oak tree, with a small house of bark built over her grave as we do. Every spring I go there and clear the grass away and leave food for her journey.

When we go west I cannot take her. A farmer will plough over that rise one day, and he will not know she is there. I have asked my daughter to remember the place, so that she can tell her children: there, under the oak, is your grandmother. But my daughter will be far away. And her children will never see the oak.

tales.title: The last sugar bush
text: This spring was the last time we made sugar at our old sugar bush on the Fox River. The maples there are older than my grandmother. We tapped them as we always have, and boiled the sap, and the children ate it on the snow, and it was a good spring.

But a man from Vermont has a paper for that land now. He came and watched us while we worked. He did not tell us to go. He only watched. I think he wanted to learn how we did it. Next spring he will tap the trees himself. I hope they give him sugar. I hope it is bitter.

tales.title: My daughter's husband
text: My daughter married a Frenchman, a trader's son, and they live in a house in the town, and their children go to the American school. By the treaty she may stay, because her husband is not one of us. Her children may stay. I must go.

She asked me to stay with her, to live in her house, to become a town woman. I could, I suppose. But I would be a stranger in her house, an old Potawatomi woman in an American kitchen. My people are going west. I will go with my people. She cried. I told her that daughters always cry and mothers always go. It is the way of the world.

tales.title: Mats for the journey
text: I am weaving new mats from the marsh rushes, more than I have ever made, to cover our lodges on the journey west and in the new country. I do not know what grows there. Maybe there are no rushes. Maybe I will need these mats for the rest of my life.

My granddaughter helps me. She is learning to split the rushes and sew them with the bone needle. Her stitches are crooked and I make her pull them out and do them again, as my grandmother did with me. She asks why it matters when we are going away. I tell her: because wherever we go, we will still be ourselves. Our stitches must still be straight.

tales.title: We are going on a long walk
text: My father says we are going on a long walk, across the whole country, to a new place where the sun goes down. It will take more days than I can count. We will take our horses and our dogs and our kettles.

I asked if there will be other children there. He said yes, many. I asked if there will be strawberries. He did not know. I asked if my friend from the town can come. He said no. I am taking my ball stick and my rabbit-skin blanket and the toy horse my grandfather carved. I am not afraid. I am a little afraid.

tales.title: The town boy and the bow
text: There is a boy in the town, with a red face and a loud voice, who wanted to learn to shoot my bow. I showed him and he shot the arrow straight into the ground. I laughed so hard I fell over.

Then I gave him the bow, because I can make another one, and he gave me a glass ball that has blue swirls inside it like the lake. I keep it in my pouch. When I look into it I can see the lake. I will take it west. There is no lake there, my father says. So I will bring one.

tales.title: My brother can read
text: My big brother went to the mission school and now he can read the Americans' words. He reads to me from a book about a man who was swallowed by a fish and spat out again. I do not believe it. My brother says it is true because it is in the book.

My grandmother says the old stories are true too, and they are not in any book. She says my brother has learned to read the Americans' words but has forgotten how to hear ours. My brother says that is not fair. I think they are both a little bit right. That is what my mother says about most arguments.

tales.title: The last of the voyageurs
text: When I came here as a young man, I paddled a canoe from Mackinac with the American Fur Company's goods, eight men to a canoe, singing all the way. In those days Chicago was a French place. The traders were French, the boatmen were French, the dances were French, the priests came from the French missions.

Now the Yankees have come, and the furs are gone, and the canoes are rotting on the bank. I work on the wharves, unloading schooners for a Yankee merchant who cannot pronounce my name. But on Saturday nights at the Sauganash, Mark Beaubien plays the old songs, and we sing them, and for an hour it is the old days again.

tales.title: The little church of St. Mary
text: Two years ago the French and the Irish of Chicago signed a letter to the bishop in St. Louis asking for a priest. There were a hundred and twenty-eight of us, more or less, though some of us signed for our children. The bishop sent Father St. Cyr, a young Frenchman, and he said the first Mass in a log cabin.

Then we built a church, a little wooden building, in a few weeks, with the new kind of thin boards nailed together. Now on Sunday mornings it is full: French, Irish, a few Germans, some of the Potawatomi families who are Catholic. The Yankees have their churches. This one is ours.

tales.title: The Beaubiens
text: There are Beaubiens everywhere in this town. Colonel Jean Baptiste Beaubien came from Detroit long ago, when Chicago was nothing, and he has married twice and has more children than a schoolroom. His brother Mark keeps the Sauganash. Their children and grandchildren are in every street.

The Colonel lives in the old house by the fort, and this spring he went into the government land office and bought the whole fort reservation for a few dollars, because he says he has lived on it longer than the soldiers. The government is furious. The Colonel just laughs. Go and see him. He is the most stubborn Frenchman in Illinois, and the kindest.

tales.title: A French dance
text: A French dance is different from a Yankee dance. The Yankees dance in rows, very correct, bowing to each other. We dance in a ring, and we spin, and we stamp, and the fiddle goes faster and faster until somebody falls down, and then everybody laughs and the fiddler starts again.

At the New Year we go from house to house, singing and dancing, and at every house there is food and wine, and you kiss everybody. The Yankees think it is scandalous. The Yankee young men come anyway. By the end of the night they are dancing in a ring and stamping too.

tales.title: The old portage man
text: Old Antoine Ouilmette was here before the first fort, when Chicago was just a river and a few houses. He carried goods across the portage for the Kinzies, and in the old war, when the soldiers marched out and were killed on the beach, he stayed in his house with his Potawatomi wife and was not harmed.

His wife was given land up the lake shore at Gros Point by the treaty, and they live up there now. He comes into town sometimes and stands on Lake Street looking at all the stores and the people, shaking his head. He says he does not recognise the place. Nobody does, any more.

tales.title: Racing in a cariole
text: In winter we French race our carioles on the frozen river, little sleighs pulled by a single horse, low and fast, with the driver standing up and the bells ringing. The Yankees have bigger sleighs, but ours are faster. Every Sunday afternoon after Mass, up and down the river from the forks to the fort.

Last winter I raced a Yankee lawyer with a fine new horse from Kentucky. He was ahead all the way until the bend by the fort, where the ice is rough. My little pony knows the ice. His big Kentucky horse did not. He went into a snowbank. I went home and bought everyone a drink.

tales.title: Family on both sides
text: My wife is half Potawatomi. Her mother's people are going west by the treaty. Her father's people, the French, are staying. My wife is staying with me and our children in Chicago. But her mother and her brothers and her cousins are going.

Every evening this summer my wife walks out to the camp by the river to sit with her mother. She comes back with red eyes and does not speak. What can I say to her? That it is the law? That it is progress? That the Americans want the land? She knows all that. What she does not know is how to say goodbye to her mother forever.

tales.title: Two peoples in one body
text: My father was a French trader and my mother is Potawatomi, and so I am both, and neither. The Americans call me a half-breed. My mother's people call me French. My father's people call me Indian. I call myself a Chicagoan, since I was born here before any of the Yankees came.

By the treaty, people like me were given land or money, because of our Indian blood. I took the money and bought a lot on Lake Street. Now I am a property owner, like a Yankee. The land my mother's people sold is paying for the land I bought. I do not know what to make of that. Nobody does.

tales.title: Turning words into other words
text: I interpret for the agent and for the traders, between the Potawatomi and the English. It is harder than it sounds. A Potawatomi chief does not say I agree. He says the words are good and the sky is clear. An American commissioner does not say you must leave. He says your Great Father wishes you to remove for your own welfare.

So I must turn one kind of speech into another, and every time I choose a word I am choosing what the other side will hear. At the great treaty I was so tired at the end of each day I could not speak at all, in any language. A good interpreter is a bridge. Everybody walks on a bridge. Nobody thanks it.

tales.title: My free papers
text: I carry my free papers in an oilcloth packet next to my skin, day and night. Under the law of this state, a Black man must show a certificate of his freedom, and if he cannot, any white man can take him up as a runaway and the sheriff can hire him out. I have shown mine twice this year, once to a constable and once to a drunk who thought he could make money from me.

This is a free state, they say, and it is, compared to Kentucky, where I was born. But free is not the same as equal. I work as a barber on Lake Street. I am good at it. The lawyers and merchants come to me because I am the best. They talk in front of me as if I were a chair. I hear everything. I say nothing.

tales.title: The first man to live here
text: The old French people tell me that the first man to make a home at the mouth of this river, the very first who was not Potawatomi, was a Black man, Jean Baptiste Point du Sable. He came from the south, from the islands, and married a Potawatomi woman and built a house and a farm on the north bank, fifty years ago. The Kinzie house was his house.

The Yankees do not talk about him. They talk about the Kinzies as if they were the first. But the old French know, and the Potawatomi know. A Black man founded Chicago. I remind the Yankees of it sometimes, when they are in my chair and I have a razor at their throat. They do not argue.

tales.title: A cook on the lake boats
text: I came here as a cook on a steamboat out of Buffalo. A good cook on a lake boat can name his wages, and the captains do not much care what colour the hands are that make the bread. I cooked for two seasons and saved my money and came ashore at Chicago.

Now I keep a little eating house near the river, for the sailors and the labourers. Fried fish, pork and beans, coffee strong enough to float a nail. Some of my customers are rough men. But a man who is hungry at five in the morning does not ask who cooked his breakfast. He asks for more.

tales.title: Waiting for my family
text: My wife and children are still in Ohio. I came ahead to find work and a place for us, and I have found both. I work for a merchant on South Water Street, loading and unloading, and he pays me fairly, the same as the white men. I have rented two rooms.

Now I am saving for their passage. It is a long way and a hard one for a Black woman with three children, through places where people would sell her if they could. I have written to a minister in Cleveland who will see them onto the boat. I count the boats coming in every day. One day, one of them will be theirs.

tales.title: Sitting in the back
text: On Sunday I go to the Methodist meeting. I sit at the back, where they want me to sit. The preacher says that all men are equal in the sight of God. Then after the meeting, the people walk past me as if I were not there.

But there is one old woman, a widow from New Hampshire, who always stops to shake my hand and ask after my health. She says that in New Hampshire she knew people who had stood up against slavery, and she means to stand up too, here, in her way. Her way is a handshake every Sunday. It is a small thing. It is not a small thing.

tales.title: The boat from Liverpool
text: I came over from Liverpool in the hold of a timber ship, with two hundred others, for six weeks. We slept on boards and ate oatmeal and drank water that tasted of the barrel. A baby was born on the way, and an old man died, and they put him over the side with a prayer and a weight at his feet.

We landed at Quebec and walked and worked our way west, by boat and on foot, through Canada and into New York and onto the lakes. It took me a year to get to Chicago. I have a dollar a day here. I have a shovel and two good arms. I will never be that hungry again.

tales.title: Waiting for the canal
text: Everybody says the canal will start next year, and when it does there will be work for ten thousand men with shovels. I am going to be one of them. Until then I unload schooners and dig foundations and carry hods of brick.

My cousin is digging on a canal in Ohio and he writes that the work is hard and the fever is worse, and men die in the ditches every summer, and the contractors cheat on the pay. I know all that. But a canal pays every week, and when it is done there will be towns along it, and lots, and a man who was there at the start can get one. I am going to be there at the start.

tales.title: Father St. Cyr
text: Father St. Cyr is a young Frenchman, and he speaks English like a Frenchman, and Irish not at all. But he is a priest, and he says Mass, and that is all that matters. Before he came there was no priest in Chicago, and a man could die without the last rites, and a baby could go unbaptized for a year.

Now we have a little church, St. Mary's, and every Sunday it is full. The French sit on one side and the Irish on the other, and the Potawatomi Catholics at the back, and Father St. Cyr preaches to all of us in his strange English. Nobody understands half of it. Everybody goes home happy.

tales.title: A fight on Lake Street
text: Last Saturday there was a fight outside a tavern on Lake Street between some Irish lads and some Yankee carpenters. It started over a girl, or a lot, or a hat, nobody remembers. It ended with eleven men in the mud and two in the doctor's office and one Irish lad with a broken nose who was very proud of it.

On Monday they were all back at work together on the same building, carrying the same beams. The Yankee who broke the Irish lad's nose bought him a drink on Tuesday. That is how it is here. You fight on Saturday and work on Monday. Nobody has time to hold a grudge. There is too much building to do.

tales.title: Patrick's luck
text: Patrick Mahoney is the luckiest man in Chicago. He came off the boat last summer with nothing but the clothes he stood up in, and the first day he found a silver dollar in the mud on Clark Street. The second day a merchant hired him. The third day he fell off a roof and landed in a hay wagon.

He says it is because his mother gave him a holy medal when he left Ireland. He shows it to everybody. Go and find him. He will show it to you, and he will tell you the hay wagon story, and by the time he is done it will have been a much higher roof.

tales.title: A lot on Lake Street
text: When I came here two years ago a man offered me a lot on Lake Street for a hundred dollars and I laughed at him. A hundred dollars for a square of mud with a frog in it! He sold it that afternoon to a fellow from Ohio.

This spring the fellow from Ohio sold it for two thousand. I know because he bought everyone in the Sauganash a drink to celebrate, and he was buying for two days. Every man in this town is a speculator now. The blacksmith, the barber, the boy who sweeps the store. They buy on paper and sell on paper and the lots never see a building. It cannot last. I said that last year too.

tales.title: The mud
text: You have not seen mud until you have seen Chicago mud in April. It is black and deep and it has no bottom. Wagons sink to the hubs on Lake Street. A man I know lost both boots in front of the post office and walked home in his stockings.

Somebody put up a board in the worst hole on Clark Street that said No Bottom Here. Somebody else, they say, stuck an old hat on top of the mud with a sign: Man Underneath. That is a joke, I hope. In July it dries out and the dust is worse. There are two seasons in this town: mud, and dust. And mosquitoes in both.

tales.title: Coming by the Erie Canal
text: I came here from Vermont by every kind of boat there is. A wagon to Albany, then the Erie Canal to Buffalo, behind a mule at four miles an hour for a week, ducking every time the steersman shouted Low bridge. Then a steamboat from Buffalo, round through the lakes, past Detroit and Mackinac, eleven days with every berth full and half the passengers sick.

When we came round the point and saw Chicago, a woman beside me burst into tears. I thought she was happy. She said: is that all? A few hundred wooden houses on a swamp. I told her it would be a great city. I do not know why I said it. I think I wanted to believe it myself.

tales.title: The drawbridge
text: The town built a drawbridge last year across the river at Dearborn Street, so the North Side people need not take the ferry. It lifts in the middle for the schooners. In theory.

In practice it is always stuck, or always up when you want it down, or a schooner comes in too fast and knocks a piece off. The North Siders love it and the South Siders hate it, because they say it brings custom to the wrong side of the river. There has been talk of pulling it down. I would not be surprised if somebody did it some night with an axe. This is not a patient town.

tales.title: The river cut through the bar
text: For years the river could not get into the lake. A sandbar lay across its mouth, and the schooners had to anchor out in the lake and send everything ashore in little boats through the surf. Then the government sent engineers to build piers and cut a channel.

Last spring the river did it for them. The ice broke up, the floods came down, and the water burst through the bar in a night. In July a schooner, the Illinois, sailed right in past the fort and tied up in the river, and the whole town came down to cheer. That was the day Chicago became a port. I was there. I cheered until I had no voice.

tales.title: A night at the Sauganash
text: If you want to see this town at its happiest, go to Mark Beaubien's Sauganash Hotel on a Saturday night. Mark plays the fiddle himself, badly and joyfully, and the whole house dances: soldiers, traders, Frenchmen, Yankees, half-breeds, lawyers, all in one room, stamping the floor until the candles jump.

He has more children than chairs and more guests than beds. If the house is full he puts you on the floor with a blanket, and if the floor is full he puts you in the barn. He never turns anyone away. Go and find him. Ask him to play the one about the girl from Detroit. He will play it whether you ask or not.

tales.title: Wolves on the prairie
text: Last winter the wolves came right up to the edge of town at night. You could hear them howling out on the prairie past the last houses, and in the morning there would be tracks in the snow right up to the pig pens.

Some of the young fellows organised a wolf hunt, on horseback, with dogs, and rode out across the frozen prairie whooping like Indians. They caught one wolf and lost two dogs and one man broke his arm falling off his horse. They called it a great success. The wolves are still out there. You can hear them some nights, even in summer.

tales.title: The ague
text: Everybody in this town has had the ague. You shake until your teeth knock together, then you burn up with fever, then you sweat, then you feel fine, and the next day it comes back at the same hour, regular as a clock. Some men shake every other day for a whole summer.

The doctors give you quinine and calomel and bleed you. Doctor Kimberly says it comes from the marsh air. Old French settlers say it is because we drink the river water. The Potawatomi have their own cures. I have tried all of them. The ague does not care. Go and see the doctor if you start to shake. He will tell you it is nothing. He will be wrong.

tales.title: Houses made of sticks
text: The old way to build a house is with great heavy timbers, cut and pegged together, and you need a dozen men and a week to raise the frame. Here they have a new way. Thin boards, two inches by four, nailed together with machine-made nails, no pegs, no joints. Two men can put up a house in a few days.

The old carpenters laughed and said a wind would blow it away like a balloon. So they call it a balloon frame. But the balloons are still standing, and there are hundreds of them now. George Snow says he thought of it. Others say it was the man who built the Catholic church. Find Mr. Snow if you like. He will tell you all about it, at length.

tales.title: Count the sails
text: This summer I have counted the sails coming in from the lake, from the top of the hill by the fort. Some days there are three, some days ten. Schooners from Buffalo and Detroit and Cleveland, full of people and barrels and boxes. Steamboats, smoking like chimneys. Every one of them goes back nearly empty, because Chicago has nothing yet to sell.

That will change, the merchants say. When the canal is dug, all the grain and pork of the Illinois country will come through here and go east on these same boats. I do not know about that. I know that I counted eleven sails yesterday, and that they were all full of people like me, coming to get rich.

tales.title: The land office sale
text: The government land office opened here this spring, and in June they began to sell the public land around Chicago at auction. You never saw such a crowd. Men came from St. Louis and Detroit and New York with saddlebags full of money, and they bid against each other on the courthouse steps like boys at a cockfight.

There were men who had squatted on their claims for years, with cabins and fences, and they stood by with rifles to make sure nobody outbid them on their own land. Nobody did. There is a sort of law here that is not in any book: you do not bid against a man on his own claim. Everybody knows it.

tales.title: The canal is coming
text: They have been talking about a canal from Chicago to the Illinois River since before I was born. Joliet talked about it, they say, a hundred and sixty years ago. Now the legislature has passed a law to borrow money to build it, and everybody says the digging will start next year.

When it comes, there will be thousands of Irishmen with shovels, and a road of water from the lake to the Mississippi, and Chicago will be the door between them. That is why everyone is buying lots. They are not buying mud. They are buying the canal. If it does not come, they are buying mud.

tales.title: The Democrat
text: When I first came, there was no newspaper. You heard the news from the last boat, and it was a month old and half wrong. Then John Calhoun brought a printing press across the lake on a schooner and started the Chicago Democrat, two years ago this winter.

It comes out once a week, four pages, and it is full of advertisements for lots and patent medicines and letters waiting at the post office, and long angry pieces about General Jackson. Paper is so scarce that some weeks he has to print on whatever he can find. Go and find Mr. Calhoun at the print shop. He will be covered in ink and complaining about the price of paper.

tales.title: A letter at the post office
text: Every week the Democrat prints the list of letters waiting at the post office, and every week I look for my name. A letter from home costs twenty-five cents to collect, and the man who gets it pays, not the man who sends it. Some letters wait for months because nobody can afford them.

Mr. Hogan keeps the post office in his store. He knows who is waiting for what, and he knows who never comes to collect. He told me once there is a letter that has been there for a year for a man nobody has ever heard of. He keeps it on a shelf, just in case. Go and ask him about it. He likes a mystery.

tales.title: Wolf Point
text: Where the river forks into the north and south branches, there is a point of land they call Wolf Point. There used to be wolves, they say. Now there are taverns. The first in Chicago was there, and the first store, and the first church meetings were held in a tavern because there was nowhere else.

Before the town was laid out on the South Side, Wolf Point was the town. Now the South Siders call it the old end of town. The Point people do not care what anyone calls them. They were here first, and they will tell you so.

tales.title: Mosquitoes
text: In July the mosquitoes come up off the marshes in clouds so thick you can hear them like a hum in the air, and they bite through your shirt, your trousers, your boots. You burn green wood in a smudge pot in the doorway to keep them out, and then you cannot breathe for the smoke, and they come in anyway.

The Potawatomi rub themselves with bear grease. It works, I am told, but you smell like a bear. My wife says she would rather be bitten than smell like a bear. I told her she could have the choice. She took the bites. I took the grease.

tales.title: Fire in a wooden town
text: This whole town is made of wood. Wooden houses, wooden stores, wooden sidewalks, wooden barns, all jammed together along Lake Street with no space between. And every one of them has a stove and a candle and a pipe-smoker inside.

Last winter a store on Water Street caught fire at night, and every man in town came running with a bucket. We made a line from the river and passed the buckets hand to hand, and we saved the buildings either side. The store burned to the ground. Somebody said it was a miracle the whole town did not go. I said, give it time. Nobody laughed.

tales.title: A carpenter can name his price
text: If you can drive a nail, you can make your fortune in Chicago this summer. Every man who has bought a lot wants a building on it yesterday. I have more work than I can do. I charge two dollars a day and they pay it, and complain, and then a fellow down the street offers three dollars and I go to him.

I came here with a chest of tools and a debt. In one year I have paid the debt and bought a lot. I live in a room behind my shop with two other men. We sleep in shifts. That is how you get rich in Chicago. Work, and do not sleep, and do not think about the future too much.

tales.title: The blacksmith's day
text: I am at the forge at five, and I do not stop until dark. Horseshoes, wagon tyres, nails, hinges, chains, ploughshares for the farmers going west. Every emigrant wagon that comes through needs something mended. Some of them need everything mended.

The Potawatomi bring me their gun locks and their kettles too. They pay in furs, or venison, or sometimes in silver brooches, which I give to my wife. She has quite a collection now. When the Potawatomi go west, and they will soon, I will miss their custom. They are better at paying than the Yankees.

tales.title: Goods from New York
text: Everything I sell comes from New York. Cloth, tea, sugar, nails, hats, shoes, crockery, books. It comes up the Hudson and along the Erie Canal and across the lakes, and by the time it gets here it costs twice what it cost in New York, and I sell it for three times.

That sounds like a fortune. It is not. Half my goods are damaged on the way. A third of my customers buy on credit and never pay. And every month a new store opens on Lake Street selling the same things for a penny less. Still, I would not go back. In New York I was a clerk. Here I am a merchant. That is worth a lot of damaged crockery.

tales.title: Sleeping under the counter
text: I am a clerk in a dry goods store on Lake Street. I sleep under the counter on a buffalo robe, with a pistol beside me in case of thieves. I open the shutters at six and close them at nine at night. I am paid a hundred dollars a year and my keep.

Every clerk in this town is going to be a merchant. We all say so. We save our money and we learn the trade and we talk about the store we will open, with our own name on the sign. Some of us will do it. Most of us will go home with the ague and a debt. I am going to do it. Everybody says that.

tales.title: A town full of lawyers
text: When I came here there were two lawyers in Chicago. Now there are a dozen, and every one of us is busy. That is what land does. Every time a lot changes hands somebody's title is wrong, somebody's boundary is in the river, somebody's deed was signed by a man who never owned it.

I spend my days in the courthouse and my nights reading. My clients pay me in lots, mostly, which means I am rich on paper and poor in my pocket, like everyone else. Mr. Caton is the best of us, though do not tell him I said so. Go and find him. He will be arguing with somebody.

tales.title: Doctoring in a new town
text: A doctor in Chicago treats everything: fevers, broken bones, gunshot wounds, babies, cholera, drunkenness, and wounds from fights over lots. I ride out to farms twenty miles away in the middle of the night through mud to my horse's belly.

Doctor Egan came here from Ireland by way of New York, and he is the best company in town. He can sing, he can tell a story, he can recite poetry by the yard, and he can set a leg while doing all three. Find him if you need a laugh. Do not find him if you need a quiet evening.

tales.title: The summer of the cholera
text: Three summers ago, in the Black Hawk war, General Scott brought his soldiers here on steamboats from the east, and they brought the cholera with them. Men who were well at breakfast were dead by supper. They turned the fort into a hospital and buried the dead in trenches on the lake shore.

The settlers who had come into the fort for safety from the Indians ran out of it again for safety from the sickness. Some of them camped on the prairie for weeks. Everybody who was here then has a name they do not say any more. If you see an old settler go quiet when someone mentions 1832, that is why.

tales.title: When the settlers ran to the fort
text: Three years ago, when Black Hawk crossed the Mississippi with his people, every farmer in northern Illinois packed his wagon and ran to Chicago. Hundreds of them, with their cattle and children and chickens, all crammed into the fort and around it. There were families sleeping under wagons on the parade ground.

Black Hawk never came anywhere near Chicago. He went up the Rock River and the army chased him into the Wisconsin country and destroyed his people at the Bad Axe. But the settlers who came here saw the lake and the river and the prairie, and some of them stayed. So in a way, Black Hawk built this town.

tales.title: Pork and beef
text: George Dole packed the first beef and pork in Chicago, three years ago, slaughtering the cattle that came in from the prairie and salting the meat in barrels to sell to the fort and ship east. People laughed at him. Who would buy beef from Chicago?

Now there are other packers, and Mr. Hubbard has a great warehouse for it, and the barrels go out on every schooner. Mark my words: one day this town will be known for its meat. The prairie grows grass, the grass grows cattle, and the cattle walk to Chicago. Go and find Mr. Dole. He will tell you exactly how many barrels he packed the first year. He remembers every one.

tales.title: The slaughterhouse on the North Branch
text: Archibald Clybourne keeps his slaughterhouse out on the North Branch, away from the town, thank heaven. He is from Virginia, and he has been here since before the town, driving cattle in from the south and butchering them for the fort and for the Indian payments.

When the wind is from the north you know exactly where his business is. But he is a good man, and an honest one, and his beef is the best in Illinois. Go and find him, if you have a strong stomach. He will tell you how to judge a steer by its walk.

tales.title: Hauling on the prairie roads
text: A teamster in Chicago hauls everything: lumber from the wharves, goods to the stores, emigrants' baggage to the wagons going west. In spring the roads are mud to the axle, and in summer the dust gets into everything, your teeth, your bread, your sleep.

Otis Bardwell drives the best team of horses in town and he will tell you so. He has been stuck in the mud on every street in Chicago at least once and he knows every hole by name. If you want to see him lose his temper, ask him about the Clark Street hole. If you want to see him smile, ask about his horses.

tales.title: A dollar a day
text: I came here because they said a labouring man could get a dollar a day in Chicago, which is twice what I got in New York. It is true. I dig foundations, I carry lumber, I unload schooners, I do whatever anybody pays for. A dollar a day.

But a room costs three dollars a week and a meal costs a quarter and flour costs twice what it does at home, so I am not as rich as I expected. Still, I have saved forty dollars since spring. When I have a hundred I am going to buy a lot. Everyone says the lots will double. Everyone cannot be wrong. Can they?

tales.title: The wagons going west
text: Every week the wagons go through. Whole families, with everything they own piled up under a canvas cover, the father walking beside the oxen, the mother on the seat with the baby, the children running behind, the cow tied to the tail. They come off the schooners and buy what they need and go out across the prairie toward the Fox River and the Rock River and Iowa.

I watch them go and I think: that was me, a year ago. And I think: one day those farms will grow wheat and send it back here to be sold. Chicago does not grow anything itself. It is a door. Everything that goes west, and everything that comes back, goes through here.

tales.title: The newcomer from New York
text: A gentleman came from New York last month, William Ogden, to look after a great piece of land his brother-in-law bought here, sight unseen. When he walked out to see it, they say, he found it was mostly under water. He went quite pale.

He is a sharp one, though. I would not bet against him. He has been walking round the town for a month with a notebook, looking at everything, asking everybody questions. Find him and tell him what you know. He will listen as if you were the only man in Chicago. That is a rare gift.

tales.title: Whiskey and the church
text: This town has more taverns than churches by about twenty to one. Whiskey is cheap and water is dirty, so men drink. Some of them drink until they lie in the mud of Lake Street, and the pigs come and sniff at them.

Philo Carpenter keeps the drugstore, and he is the most religious man in Chicago. He started a Sunday school and he wants everybody to sign the pledge and give up drink. Some of us have. Some of us signed it in the morning and drank it away by the evening. Go and see Mr. Carpenter. He will be very kind to you, and he will hand you a pamphlet.

tales.title: Setting type by candlelight
text: I set type for the newspaper. Every letter of every word, picked out of the case by hand, backwards, and locked into the frame. A good compositor sets a thousand letters an hour. I am a good compositor.

On the night before the paper comes out we work until three in the morning by candlelight, inking and pulling the press, two hundred copies, four hundred, until our arms ache. Then I walk home in the dark with ink on my hands and the smell of it in my clothes. My landlady says I smell like a newspaper. I tell her I am one.

tales.title: Every bed full
text: Every boat brings more people than this town has beds. I have twelve rooms and I put three men to a bed and six to a floor, and still I turn people away. They sleep in the barn, in the woodshed, on the porch. One man slept in a barrel last week.

I charge what I like, and they pay it. Some of them grumble. I tell them: go to the next house, and they come back an hour later because the next house is fuller than mine. This is the best business in Chicago, while it lasts. When the boom ends, the hotels will be the first to know.

tales.title: What you hear in a tavern
text: Keep a tavern long enough and you know everything about everybody. Who bought which lot, who sold it, who owes money to whom, who is courting whose daughter, who has the ague, who is drinking too much, who is going west.

I do not repeat any of it. That is the first rule of a tavern keeper. The second rule is to keep the whiskey and the fighting on different sides of the room. The third rule is never to lend money to a land speculator. I have broken the third rule more times than I can count.

tales.title: Drawing lines on the prairie
text: I am a surveyor. I walk out on the prairie with a chain and a compass and I draw lines where there are no lines. Here is a street, here is a lot, here is a corner. Then a man buys the lot, and builds on it, and my line becomes a real thing, a wall, a fence, a quarrel.

The town was first laid out on paper five years ago by a man named Thompson, for the canal commissioners. Every street in Chicago today is on his map. Some of them are still only on his map. The rest of the world is catching up with the paper, one lot at a time.

tales.title: Who owns the fort's land?
text: The land around the fort belongs to the government, everybody knows that. But Jean Baptiste Beaubien has lived on part of it for years, and this spring he went into the land office and bought the whole fort reservation, all of it, for less than a hundred dollars, under the law that lets a settler buy the land he lives on.

The government says he cannot do that. He says he has done it, and here is his receipt. It will go to the courts, and the lawyers will get rich, and in the meantime the soldiers drill on Beaubien's land. Go and ask the Colonel about it. He will laugh and show you the receipt.

tales.title: I remember when there was nothing here
text: When I came here in 1829 there were a dozen houses and the fort. Everybody knew everybody. There were more Indians than whites and more French than Yankees. We had dances at the Kinzie house and the fort, and the only road was the Indian trail.

Now there are three thousand people and I do not know half the faces on Lake Street. Everybody is in a hurry. Everybody is buying and selling. Nobody has time for a dance. I am not complaining. I own four lots and they have made me richer than I ever dreamed. But I miss the old place, sometimes. I miss knowing everybody.

tales.title: Money made of paper
text: There is not enough real money in this town. Gold and silver are scarce as diamonds. So everybody pays in paper: bank notes from Michigan and Ohio and Indiana banks, some of them good, some of them worth half, some of them printed by banks that do not exist.

A merchant keeps a little book that tells him which notes are good this week. A man can be rich on Monday and poor on Friday because a bank in Detroit has failed. General Jackson has made war on the national bank, so now every little bank prints its own money. It is madness. But it is profitable madness, so nobody complains.

tales.title: The steamboat whistle
text: When a steamboat comes in, the whole town knows it. You hear the whistle from far out on the lake, and then you see the smoke, and every boy in Chicago runs down to the river mouth to watch her come in past the piers.

Then the passengers come ashore, pale and seasick, with their trunks and their children and their dreams, and the hotel keepers fight over them like gulls over a fish. I watched it from the pier last week. A man stepped off the boat, looked around at the mud and the shanties, and asked the nearest fellow where the city was. The fellow said: you are standing in it.

tales.title: The fort at the end of the street
text: Fort Dearborn sits at the end of the town by the lake, its pickets and two blockhouses, and the flag over it. The soldiers come into town on their days off and spend their pay in the taverns, and the officers come to the dances.

There are old settlers who remember the first fort, the one that was burned in the war. They say it stood in the same place. They say the people who were killed are buried somewhere along the lake shore to the south, and nobody knows exactly where. When the wind blows in from the lake on a summer night and the sand moves, sometimes, they say, you find things.

tales.title: Preaching in a warehouse
text: There was no church in Chicago until two years ago. Before that the preachers held meetings wherever they could: in a tavern, in a warehouse, in the fort's carpenter shop. Now there are a handful of congregations, Presbyterian, Baptist, Methodist, Episcopal and Catholic, all trying to build churches as fast as the taverns.

The Catholics built theirs in a few weeks, of light boards nailed together, and everybody said it would fall down. It did not. The Methodists preached on the street corner last Sunday and a man drove his cattle right through the congregation. The preacher did not stop. Neither did the cattle.

tales.title: Our first winter
text: We came in October, on the last schooner of the year, and my husband had not built the house yet. We lived in a shanty of rough boards with a canvas roof, my husband and I and three children and a stove. In January the snow blew in through the cracks and lay on the quilts in the morning like sugar.

The lake froze out as far as you could see. No boats came for five months. No letters, no news, no fresh food. We ate salt pork and potatoes and corn bread every day from Christmas to April. In April the first schooner came round the point and every woman in town went down to the river to cry. I was one of them.

tales.title: Shopping on Lake Street
text: When I came here two years ago there was one store worth the name. Now there are forty on Lake Street and South Water Street, and you can buy anything if you can pay for it: silk from France, tea from China, a piano from Boston, a bonnet in the latest New York style, only a season late.

But you cannot buy fresh milk, or a decent egg, or a vegetable that has not travelled a thousand miles. I keep my own cow behind the house and my own hens and a garden. My neighbours laugh at me. Then they come and ask to buy my eggs. I charge them twice what the store does. They pay it.

tales.title: Twelve boarders and one stove
text: I keep a boarding house. Twelve men, three to a room, two meals a day and a cold supper. I cook on one stove in a kitchen the size of a wagon. I bake twelve loaves every morning. I buy a barrel of flour every week and a barrel of pork every month and I scrub the floors on Saturday.

My boarders are clerks and carpenters and young lawyers, all of them going to be rich next year. They pay me three dollars a week, when they pay. I have one who has owed me since March. He tells me he has bought a lot that will be worth a fortune by the fall, and he will pay me then with interest. I have heard that before.

tales.title: Washing for the town
text: I wash for six families and two hotels. Monday I collect the bundles. Tuesday I boil. Wednesday I scrub and rinse and wring. Thursday I hang it out on the lines behind my house, and pray it does not rain, and pray the dust does not blow. Friday I iron with irons heated on the stove. Saturday I deliver.

On Sunday I rest, and my hands crack and bleed from the lye. I am paid fifty cents a dozen pieces. It is more than I could get anywhere else. My husband died last year of the fever. This is how I feed my children. I am not complaining. I am only telling you why my hands look the way they do.

tales.title: The latest fashion
text: I am a dressmaker, and every lady in Chicago wants a dress like the ones in the New York magazines, with sleeves as big as hams and a waist as small as a wrist. The magazines arrive three months late, and so the fashions do too, and the ladies do not know it, and I do not tell them.

I learned my trade in Albany. Here I can charge double what I could there, because there are only three of us and two hundred ladies who suddenly have money. I have taken on two girls to help me. If this goes on I will have a shop of my own on Lake Street by next spring. A woman can do that here. Not many places she can.

tales.title: Bonnets
text: A bonnet tells you everything about a woman in this town. A plain straw one with a ribbon: a farmer's wife, just off the boat, going west. A silk one with feathers: a merchant's wife, three months in town and making sure everyone knows her husband has done well.
