I make both kinds. I prefer making the plain ones, if I am honest. The farmers' wives are so grateful, and they hold the bonnet in both hands as if it were made of glass. The merchants' wives complain that the feathers are not tall enough. I make the feathers taller. They complain about the price.

tales.title: Hired girl in a Yankee house
text: I am a hired girl. I cook and clean and carry water and mind the children for a lawyer's family on the South Side. I sleep in the attic and I have Sunday afternoons to myself. I am paid a dollar and a half a week, which is more than my father earned in Ireland in a month.

The mistress is kind but she watches me as if I might steal the spoons. In Yankee houses they think every Irish girl is a Catholic spy. I am a Catholic. I am not a spy. Go and meet Mary Flynn, who works on the next street. She has a worse mistress than mine and a better sense of humour.

tales.title: The cow on the prairie
text: Every family that can afford one keeps a cow, and in the morning the cows go out on the prairie to graze, and in the evening a boy goes out to bring them back. Except the cows do not come back. They wander miles. They get stuck in the marshes. They get taken by wolves, or by people who are not wolves.

My cow, Beatrice, has a bell on her neck so I can hear her. Last week the bell came home without her. A man brought her back three days later and asked for a dollar for his trouble. I am almost certain he was the one who took her. I paid him. You must pick your battles in this town.

tales.title: The school in the church
text: There are more children in Chicago than benches to put them on. The first school was only three years ago, when John Watkins taught a dozen children in a little log building. Now there are several, in churches and storerooms and rented rooms, and still not enough.

I teach thirty children in a room meant for fifteen. They are from everywhere: Vermont, Ohio, Ireland, Canada, one little French girl who speaks no English at all. I teach them reading and arithmetic and geography, and they teach me how to break up a fight between a Yankee and an Irish boy without being knocked down. Go and see Mr. Watkins. He will tell you how it was in the old days.

tales.title: A dance at the fort
text: When the officers at the fort hold a dance, every lady in town is invited, and there are four gentlemen for every lady, so you dance until your feet bleed. The music is a fiddle and a flute, and sometimes a soldier with a drum who cannot keep time.

At the last dance I danced with a lieutenant, a land agent, two lawyers, a doctor, a fur trader with a scar on his face, and Mr. Beaubien, who dances like a whirlwind and sings at the same time. My husband danced with nobody, because there was nobody left. He sat by the punch bowl and talked about lots. He enjoyed himself, he says.

tales.title: A letter to my mother
text: I write to my mother in Connecticut every week, and every week I try to make Chicago sound like a place she would approve of. I tell her about the churches and the school and the ladies' sewing circle. I do not tell her about the mud, or the drunks in the street, or the wolves, or the Indians camped on the edge of town.

She writes back and asks when I am coming home. I do not know how to tell her that I am not coming home. That this is home now, with all its mud. That I like it here, God help me. That I have never felt so alive.

tales.title: A baby born in Chicago
text: My baby was born in March, in our house on Clark Street, with the snow blowing against the windows. The doctor came through the drifts on horseback and arrived just in time to say congratulations. My neighbour, Mrs. Hamilton, delivered her. She has delivered a dozen babies in this town.

She is a Chicago baby. She will grow up here. She will never know a place without the lake. When she is old, I suppose, Chicago will be a great city, and she will tell her grandchildren that she remembers when it was a few wooden houses in the mud. They will not believe her.

tales.title: Water from the lake
text: The river water is filthy. Everything goes into it: the slops, the slaughterhouse, the stables. So the water carrier brings water from the lake in a cart with a barrel, and sells it by the bucket, door to door. A shilling a barrel.

I cannot afford a barrel every day for my washing. So I go down to the lake myself with two buckets on a yoke, three times a morning, a quarter mile each way. My shoulders are like a man's now. My husband says I could beat him at arm wrestling. I could. I have not told him so.

tales.title: The sewing circle
text: The ladies of the Presbyterian church have a sewing circle on Thursday afternoons. We sew for the poor, and for the missionaries, and for the new church we are trying to build, and we talk about everybody who is not in the room.

It is the only time in the week I sit down. It is the only time I talk to other women about something besides the price of flour. Last week we talked for an hour about whether it was proper for a lady to walk on Lake Street alone in the afternoon. We decided it was not. Then we all walked home along Lake Street alone. That is Chicago.

tales.title: Sending money home
text: Every month I send three dollars home to my mother in County Cork, sewn into the lining of a letter. It takes two months to get there. Sometimes it does not get there at all. My brothers and sisters eat because I work in a Yankee kitchen in a town at the end of the world.

My mother writes, through the priest, that the potatoes were bad again last year and that half the village has gone to America. She says I am a good girl. I do not feel like a good girl. I feel like a tired one. But on Sunday I go to Mass at the little church and I light a candle, and for an hour I feel like I am home.

tales.title: A widow in a boom town
text: My husband died last summer of the ague, six weeks after we arrived. I had two children, a trunk of clothes, eleven dollars and a lot on the North Side that he had bought the week before he died.

Everybody told me to go home. I did not. I sold the lot in the spring for four hundred dollars, which is more money than I had seen in my life, and I rented a house and took in boarders. Now I have six and a hired girl. I am not rich. But I am not going home, either. This town gave me a second chance. I do not intend to waste it.

tales.title: Nursing the sick
text: In the summer, when the fevers come, every woman in town is a nurse. You go next door with a basket of broth and clean linen, and you sit up all night with your neighbour's husband while she sleeps, and the next week she does the same for you.

There are not enough doctors, and the ones there are often worse than none. So the women do it. We know which herbs ease a fever and which ones only make you feel better. We know when to send for the minister. I have sat with eleven people who were dying, in three years. I remember every one of their names.

tales.title: The hens and the pigs
text: Pigs run loose in the streets of Chicago. Nobody knows who owns half of them. They root in the mud and sleep under the sidewalks and eat anything that is dropped. They are the town's garbage collectors, my husband says.

They also ate three of my hens last month, and my whole row of beans, and a pair of my husband's boots that he left on the porch. I chased one down Clark Street with a broom in my nightgown. The neighbours still talk about it. I do not care. I got one boot back.

tales.title: My Potawatomi neighbour
text: When we first came, a Potawatomi family camped near our house on the North Side for the summer, and the woman used to come to my door with baskets of berries to trade. I gave her flour and needles. She gave me berries and maple sugar and once a pair of moccasins for my baby that were the most beautiful thing I have ever owned.

We could not speak to each other. We used our hands and laughed a lot. This summer she came again, and when I tried to ask about next year, she shook her head and pointed west, and made a motion with her hand like a long road. Then she gave me the berries and would not take anything for them.

tales.title: A frame house with a piano
text: My husband built us a frame house last year, two storeys, white-painted, with green shutters and a picket fence, the finest on our street. He ordered a piano from Boston and it came round the lakes in a crate, and four men carried it up from the river.

It is out of tune. There is no one in Chicago who can tune it. I play it anyway, on summer evenings, with the windows open, and people stop in the street to listen. I am not a good player. But I am the only one on the street with a piano, and so I am the best. That is how it is in a new town.

tales.title: The hotel keeper's wife
text: My husband keeps the hotel, they say. My husband greets the guests and drinks with them and tells stories. I keep the hotel. I cook for forty people, wash for forty people, make forty beds, and keep the accounts, because he cannot add.

I have four children and two hired girls and a cook who drinks. I sleep five hours a night. When a guest says what a fine house your husband keeps, I smile and say thank you. Then I go and find out which guest broke the window in room six.

tales.title: Sleighing on the river
text: In winter, when the river freezes solid, everybody goes out sleighing. You hire a sleigh and a horse and race up and down the river and out onto the lake ice, with buffalo robes over your knees and the bells jingling. Young men race each other. Everybody shouts.

Last winter a sleigh went through the ice near the mouth of the river, where the current keeps it thin. The horse drowned. The two young men got out, soaked and freezing, and walked into the Sauganash looking like icicles. Mr. Beaubien gave them hot whiskey and played them a song about it. They are still telling the story. So is everybody else.

tales.title: Going on west
text: We are only stopping in Chicago for a week. My husband has bought a quarter section on the Fox River, sight unseen, and we are going out there with a wagon and two oxen, five children and a cow. I have never seen it. He has never seen it. A land agent showed him a map.

I asked him what we will do if it is a swamp. He said we will drain it. I asked what if there is no water. He said we will dig a well. I asked what if the Indians come. He said they are going west, too, far beyond us. I did not ask any more questions. I am going to buy needles and thread and seeds and a Bible, and pray.

tales.title: Mrs. Kinzie's parlour
text: Mrs. John Kinzie is the most interesting woman in Chicago. She came from Connecticut, married Mr. Kinzie, and went to live at a fort in the Wisconsin wilderness among the Winnebago, where her husband was the agent. She rode horseback through the forests in winter with a baby. She tells the best stories of anyone.

Her husband's family were here at the first fort, in the old war, and his mother told her everything that happened. Mrs. Kinzie says she means to write it all down someday. I hope she does. Go and call on her if you can. She will give you tea and tell you something that will keep you awake at night.

tales.title: The lad from Galway
text: There is a lad from Galway who works on the harbour piers, and he walks past my mistress's kitchen door every evening and says good evening, and I say good evening, and that is all. For a month. Good evening, good evening.

Last Sunday after Mass he walked me home and asked if he could call on me. I said he could. My mistress says an Irish girl should not walk out with an Irish labourer, she should marry a respectable Yankee mechanic. I said, with respect, ma'am, I will marry who I like. She did not speak to me for two days. I did not care. He is calling on Sunday.

allen_lieut_james.title: Taming the river mouth
text: I am an officer of the infantry, and for two years I have been an engineer too, because somebody had to build the piers at the mouth of this river, and I was here. Great cribs of timber, filled with stone, run out into the lake to keep the channel open.

The river is a stubborn creature. It wants to go south along the beach, the way the sand drifts, and close its own mouth. The piers push it straight out. In a big storm the lake throws everything back at us. One day there will be a harbour here as good as Buffalo. I will not be here to see it. The army moves its lieutenants about like chess pieces.

beaubien_jean_baptiste.title: I bought the fort
text: I came to Chicago more than twenty years ago as a trader, and I have lived on this land beside the fort for most of that time, in the old house I bought from Charles Lee's widow. So this spring, when the land office opened, I went in and entered the whole fort reservation in my name, as a settler living on it. All of it, for less than a hundred dollars. Here is my receipt.

The government says it is theirs. The major is very angry. The lawyers are very happy. I say: the law says a man may buy the land he lives on, and I have lived on it longer than any soldier now at the fort. Go and ask Major Greene what he thinks. Stand back a little when he answers.

beaubien_josette.title: I was in the boat
text: Twenty-three years ago, in the summer of the old war, I was nurse to the Kinzie children, a girl of French and Ottawa family. On the morning the soldiers marched out of the first fort, I sat in the Kinzies' boat at the river mouth with Mrs. Kinzie and the little ones, and we watched the column go down the shore. I will not tell you what we saw.

Afterwards I married Jean Baptiste Beaubien, and I have raised his children and my own in this town ever since. The boy I minded in that boat, John Kinzie, is a grown man now with a business on the river. Go and find him. Ask him if he remembers the pockets I sewed into his clothes, with corn and sugar inside. He will remember.

beaubien_mark.title: I keep tavern
text: I came here from Detroit nine years ago, following my brother the Colonel, and I bought a log house by the forks of the river and started keeping tavern. Then I built the Sauganash next to it, named for my friend Billy Caldwell, and painted it white with blue shutters, the finest house in Chicago for a while.

I play the fiddle. Not well, but loud, and long, and nobody leaves my house without dancing. I have more children than I can count without using both hands twice, and more guests than beds, and I have never turned a man away. If a man has no money, he eats anyway. My brother says I will die poor. I say I will die happy. Go and find my brother. He will tell you I am a fool, and then he will laugh.

caldwell_billy.title: Sauganash
text: They call me Sauganash, the Englishman. My father was an Irish officer in the King's service, and my mother's people were of this country, and I have lived my life between the two. In the old war I rode with Tecumseh. Afterwards I made my peace, and the Americans made me a justice of the peace here in Chicago, which amuses me still.

Two years ago at the great treaty I spoke for the united bands, and signed. Some of our people say I sold them. I say I got them what could be got, and land in the west, when the alternative was nothing and a soldier's bayonet. Within three years they must go. I will go with them. Go and find Robinson. He signed too. Ask him if we did right.

calhoun_john.title: A press across the lake
text: I brought a printing press, type, ink and paper across the lake on a schooner two years ago, and I set up the Chicago Democrat in a little building on South Water Street. The first issue came out in November of 1833, and there were so few people in town who could pay for it that I printed for the whole Northwest, by mail.

Paper is my curse. It comes from the east, round the lakes, and when the boats stop in winter I run out, and I have had to print on whatever paper I could buy or beg. Every week I print the list of letters waiting at the post office. Go and see Mr. Hogan. Without his letters and my list, half this town would never hear from home.

carpenter_philo.title: The first druggist
text: I came here in 1832 with a stock of drugs and medicines and opened the first drugstore in Chicago, in a log building at Lake Street. Quinine for the ague, calomel for the fevers, laudanum for pain, and a great many patent remedies that do more good to the seller than the buyer.

But my real work is the Sunday school. I started it to teach the children of this town to read, and to know their Bible, in a place where there was no school and no church. There are a great many children here and not enough teachers. Go and see Mr. Watkins. He taught the first school in Chicago. He can tell you how many children there were then, and how many there are now.

caton_john_dean.title: The young lawyer
text: I came here two years ago, a young lawyer with no clients and a borrowed suit, and I tried one of the first jury cases in Chicago in a room over a store, with the jurors sitting on barrels. Now I cannot keep up with the work.

Every case in this town is about land. Who owns it, where its lines run, whether the man who sold it had any right to sell. I have had clients who bought the same lot from three different men. I have had a lot that turned out to be in the river. The law has not caught up with Chicago. I am trying to help it.

clybourne_archibald.title: Beef for the fort
text: I came from Virginia as a young man, before there was any town at all, and I drove cattle up from the south to sell to the fort. I built a slaughterhouse on the North Branch, which is still there, and I have supplied beef to the garrison and to the Indian payments for years.

At the great treaty two years ago I sold beef to feed eight thousand Indians for two weeks. I have never been so busy in my life. Now George Dole and Hubbard ship meat east by the barrel. I sell mostly to the town. There is room enough for all of us. Go and see Dole. Ask him who sold him his first steers.

dole_george_w.title: The first packer
text: I came here in 1831 and opened a store, and in 1832 I slaughtered and packed the first beef and pork that was ever shipped out of Chicago. A hundred and fifty head of cattle and some hogs, salted in barrels, sent east by schooner. Everybody thought I was mad.

Now Mr. Hubbard packs more than I do, and others besides, and the barrels go out every week in the season. The prairie is all grass, and the grass will feed cattle, and the cattle will walk to Chicago. Mark my words: this town will be the great meat market of the West. Go and see Hubbard. He thinks he invented it.

egan_william_b.title: An Irish doctor
text: I came from Ireland by way of New York and Newark, two years ago, and I took one look at Chicago and decided it was the most ridiculous and wonderful place I had ever seen. I have not changed my mind.

I treat the rich and the poor, the Yankees and the Irish, the soldiers and the sailors. I have set legs, delivered babies, pulled teeth, and once removed a fishhook from a judge. I sing at dinners and give speeches at the Fourth of July and argue politics with anyone who will stand still. Go and see Dr. Kimberly. He is a better doctor than I am. I am a better guest.

greene_john.title: Commanding the fort
text: I command Fort Dearborn and its garrison, a few dozen men of the infantry, and I have commanded harder posts with fewer comforts. But I have never commanded a post where the enemy was a land office.

The town presses on my walls from every side. My soldiers desert to become carpenters. The taverns sell them whiskey at the gate. And now Colonel Beaubien has bought the fort reservation out from under me with a receipt from the land office. I have written to Washington. Washington has not answered. Go and see the Colonel. Tell him I said good day. He will know what I mean.

hamilton_richard_j.title: Every office in the county
text: I came here in 1831 and they made me clerk of the county court, recorder of deeds, probate judge, and commissioner of schools, all at once, because there was nobody else who could write a fair hand. I had six jobs and one desk.

Now every deed for every lot in Chicago comes through my office. I record them all, in big leather books, in ink, by hand. Some lots have changed hands five times since the spring. I see the price go up every time. One lot I recorded at a hundred dollars last year was sold this week for three thousand. I wrote it down without a word. Then I went home and lay down for an hour.

hogan_john_s_c.title: The postmaster
text: I keep the post office, in a corner of my store, with a set of pigeon holes for the letters and a ledger for the money. When the mail comes, by horseback from the south or by boat from the east, the whole town crowds into my store to see if there is anything for them.

There are letters here that have waited a year. Letters for men who have died, or gone west, or never arrived at all. Love letters. Letters with money in them. Letters from mothers. I cannot open them, and I cannot throw them away. So they wait. Mr. Calhoun prints the list in his paper every week. Go and see him. Tell him the list is getting longer.

hubbard_gurdon.title: The Swift Walker
text: I came to Chicago at sixteen, in 1818, a clerk for the American Fur Company, in a canoe from Mackinac. The Potawatomi called me Swift Walker, because I could walk seventy-five miles in a day. I married into the Kankakee band and traded all through the Illinois country.

In 1827, when there was a scare that the Winnebago were rising, I rode a hundred and twenty-five miles to Danville in a day and a night to bring the militia. Now I have a warehouse on the river and I pack pork and beef for the east, and I have more lots than I can walk to in a day. I knew John Kinzie the elder. His son is my friend. Go and find him. Tell him Hubbard says the canal will come.

kimberly_edmund_s.title: A doctor in the mud
text: I came here in 1832 and I was one of the first doctors in Chicago. That summer the cholera came with General Scott's soldiers, and I learned more medicine in a month than in all my years of study, and buried more patients than I like to remember.

Now the ague is my daily bread. Every second patient shakes. I give quinine and calomel and tell them to drink lake water, not river water, and to keep their windows shut at night against the marsh air. Some of them listen. Dr. Egan, my colleague, thinks I am too gloomy. Go and see him. He will tell you nobody ever died of laughing.

kinzie_john_h.title: The boy in the boat
text: I was nine years old in August 1812, the eldest of my father's children, sitting in the family boat at the mouth of the river while the soldiers marched out. My father walked with the column. My half-sister rode beside her husband. Josette, our nurse, held my baby brother. I remember the sound more than the sight.

My father lived, by the help of his Potawatomi friends. He died seven years ago, here in Chicago. Now I am in the forwarding and commission business on the river, and I have been president of the town board, and I live a few hundred yards from where I sat in that boat. Go and find Madame Beaubien. She was Josette then. She still calls me Johnny.

kinzie_juliette.title: The agent's wife
text: I came from Connecticut as a bride five years ago and went with my husband to Fort Winnebago in the Wisconsin country, where he was agent to the Winnebago. I rode through the forests in winter with my baby, slept in bark lodges, and learned more in three years than in my whole life before.

Now we are in Chicago, which is a very different kind of wilderness. My husband's mother told me before she died everything she remembered of the old fort and the war, and I have it all in my head, and some of it on paper. One day I may write it down properly. Go and meet my husband. He was in that story, as a boy. He does not tell it. I do.

newberry_walter_loomis.title: Buying land
text: I came here two years ago from Detroit and I have bought land, and land, and more land. Some people say I am a fool. Some people say I am a genius. Both groups are waiting to see which, and so am I.

I do not buy lots on Lake Street for two thousand dollars. I buy acres on the North Side for a few dollars each, out where there is nothing but prairie, and I wait. The town is coming that way. I can see it from my window, one house at a time. Go and meet Mr. Ogden, the new man from New York. He thinks the way I do. One day he will own half of Chicago, and I will own the other half.

ogden_w_b.title: Under water
text: I came here from New York only last month, to look after a tract of land my brother-in-law bought sight unseen. When I walked out to see it, I found most of it under water. I wrote to him that he had been badly sold.

And yet. I have been walking this town for a month now, and talking to everybody, and I begin to think I was wrong. There is a river, a lake, a portage, and a prairie that goes all the way to the Mississippi. When the canal comes, this will be the gate of the whole West. I may stay a while. Go and see Mr. Newberry. He has been here two years and he has bought more land than anybody.

peck_philip.title: The first frame store
text: I came here in 1831 with a stock of goods on a schooner, and I put up one of the first frame buildings in Chicago, a store on South Water Street with my living quarters above it. Before that everything was logs.

I have sold to the Potawatomi and the French, to the soldiers and the settlers, to everyone who has come through this town in four years. I have bought lots with my profits, and the lots have made me richer than the store. But I still open the shutters every morning at six, because a merchant who stops minding his store is no longer a merchant. He is a speculator. I do not want to be a speculator. Mostly.

rc_bardwell_otis.title: My horses
text: I am a teamster. I have the best two horses in Chicago, Dan and Duke, bay geldings out of Kentucky, and I would not sell them for a lot on Lake Street. I haul lumber from the wharves and goods to the stores and baggage to the emigrant wagons, from dawn to dark.

In the spring I got stuck in the great hole on Clark Street with a load of bricks, and it took six men and two more teams to pull me out. I lost half the bricks. They are still down there, I expect, at the bottom of the mud. Some day a man will dig a cellar there and find them and wonder. Go and see Patrick Mahoney. He was one of the six. He fell in.

rc_flynn_mary.title: My mistress's spoons
text: I am a hired girl in a Yankee lawyer's house. I came from County Cork with my brothers last year. I cook, scrub, wash, iron, mind the children and carry the water, from five in the morning until nine at night. I have Sunday afternoons and every second Thursday.

My mistress counts the spoons every night after supper. Every night. I have never taken so much as a crust. One night I counted them for her before she could start, and told her the number, and she went red and did not count them again for a week. Go and find Patrick Mahoney. He is from the next parish to mine at home. He will tell you I have a temper. That is a lie. Mostly.

rc_mahoney_patrick.title: The hay wagon
text: I came off the boat last summer with nothing, and on my first morning in Chicago I found a silver dollar in the mud. My mother gave me a holy medal when I left Cork, and I have had nothing but luck since.

On the third day I was working on a roof on Lake Street and I fell off it. Two storeys. And I landed flat in a hay wagon that was passing just at that moment, and the driver did not even notice, and he drove me halfway to Wolf Point before I sat up. Go and ask Mary Flynn. She saw it. She says it was one storey. She is jealous of my luck.

robinson_alexander.title: Che-che-pin-qua
text: I am Alexander Robinson. My father was a Scotsman and my mother was Odawa, and the Potawatomi call me Che-che-pin-qua. I have traded in this country since before the old war. In 1812, after the battle, my wife and I paddled the wounded captain and his wife all the way up the lake to Mackinac to get them to safety.

By the treaties I have a reservation on the Des Plaines, and I will stay there when the people go. Some of them hold that against me. I signed the great treaty two years ago, with Billy Caldwell, because I believed it was better than what would happen if we did not. I still believe it. Go and see Billy. He will tell you the same. He sounds better when he says it.

watkins_john.title: The first school
text: I taught the first school in Chicago, three years ago, in a little log building on the North Side. I had twelve pupils, and only four of them were children of Yankee families; the rest were French and Potawatomi children of the old trading families, and none of them had ever been in a school before.

We had no books worth the name and no slates and no benches. I taught them their letters on boards with charcoal. One of the French boys learned to read in a month and then taught his mother. Now there are many schools and many teachers, and I am very proud. Go and see Mr. Carpenter. His Sunday school taught as many children as I did.

asks.q: What does a soldier earn here?
a: Six dollars a month and rations, paid when the paymaster comes, which is when he feels like it. A carpenter in town makes a dollar and a half a day. You can do the sum. Every man in this barracks does it every night.

Because a man who runs is a deserter and they put his name in the papers with a reward. Because the army feeds you when the town does not. Because I signed. The major knows what the town does to his men. He cannot pay us more and he cannot build a wall high enough. Go and ask him how many he lost this spring.
Carpentry. I can frame a wall as well as any man in Chicago. My enlistment is up next year. Then I shall be in town with a hammer and a lot of my own, if there are any lots left.

asks.q: Is it true someone bought the fort?
a: Colonel Beaubien went into the land office this spring and entered the whole fort reservation in his name, as the man living on it, for less than a hundred dollars. He has a receipt. The major has a fort. Washington has a headache. The lawyers in town have never been happier.

He says the law lets a settler buy the land he lives on, and he has lived on it longer than any of us have been soldiers. The major says a fort is not a farm. I say I would like to see the Colonel try to evict a company of infantry. Go and ask him how he means to do it. He will laugh and offer you a glass.

asks.q: What do you watch for on sentry at night?
a: Fire, mostly. A whole town of wooden houses outside the walls, and every one of them has a stovepipe through a roof. After that, soldiers coming back from the taverns over the pickets, and townsmen trying to sell whiskey through the gate. The enemy is not out on the prairie any more. He is on Lake Street with a jug.

The lake at night is not dull. You stand on the blockhouse and the water is black and the light at the harbour mouth is the only thing out there. On a calm night you hear the waves on the sand and the frogs in the slough and the fiddle at the Sauganash. On a stormy one you hear nothing but the wind.

asks.q: How many stars are on that flag?
a: Twenty-four, one for every state, Missouri the last. Thirteen stripes. We raise it at dawn and strike it at sunset with the gun, and the whole town sets its clocks by us. It is the one thing about this fort that nobody has bought yet.

Michigan wants one, and Arkansas, and they say Michigan and Ohio nearly went to war this spring over a strip of land at Toledo. Imagine it: two states fighting over a swamp. Out here we would sell them a better swamp for less.

asks.q: Were you here for the Black Hawk war?
a: I came in with General Scott's army in thirty-two, on the steamboats from the East, and the cholera came with us. We lost more men to it on the way here and in this fort than the whole war lost to the Sauk. They buried them by the lake.

I never saw him. By the time we were well enough to march, the militia had chased him across Wisconsin to the Mississippi and it was over. I saw his people afterwards, though, and that was enough. Starving women. Children with no shoes. I do not boast about that summer.

asks.q: What do you do off duty?
a: Fish off the pier. Whitefish, perch, pike, now and then a sturgeon big enough to feed the company. The officers hunt ducks in the slough. The men play cards and drink if they can get it, and walk out with the town girls if they can get that. Mostly they can get the fish.

The end of the north pier, early, when the water is flat. A sergeant showed me. He has fished this river mouth since the fort was rebuilt, and he swears the perch know his voice. Bring a line and come at dawn and I will show you.

asks.q: Do the soldiers marry town girls?
a: Some do. A private needs his captain's leave and he will not get it unless the girl can wash for the company. There are more men in this town than women by three to one, so a girl can choose, and she does not choose a private at six dollars a month if she can get a carpenter.
There is a girl at the boarding house on Lake Street who gives me an extra potato. That is all I am saying. In Chicago an extra potato is practically a proposal.

asks.q: Where were you posted before?
a: Fort Brady, at the Sault, at the top of Lake Huron, where the winter lasts eight months and the snow comes over the pickets. Before that Fort Howard at Green Bay. This is the softest post I have had: a town at the gate, fresh beef, and the boats in all summer.

I prefer it to the Sault. But at the Sault a man knew what he was there for. Here the fort guards nothing but itself. The Potawatomi are going west, the town has three thousand people and its own sheriff. The word is that they will close the fort and send us off before long. I believe it.

asks.q: Who plays the drum at the fort?
a: A boy of sixteen from Ohio and a fifer who used to be a sailor. They play the calls all day and the town knows every one: reveille, breakfast, drill, dinner, retreat, tattoo. A merchant on Water Street told me he does not need a clock any more, he has the fort.

more.q: Do they ever play for fun?
a: On the Fourth of July they play everything they know, in the square, and the town dances. That is three days from now. Come and see it. There will be a salute from the gun and speeches from every lawyer in town and the soldiers will be very thirsty by evening.

asks.q: What's it like being an officer here?
a: Strange. I have a commission, a sword, and a company of men who would rather be carpenters. The town invites me to every supper and every ball because an officer in a blue coat makes a room look respectable. The rest of the time I write reports nobody reads.

Lieutenant Allen, who builds the harbour. He is the only one of us doing something the town will remember. He is out on the pier every morning with his pole, measuring the depth of the channel. Go and ask him how deep it is today. He will know to the inch.

asks.q: What did your people get in the treaty?
a: Land west of the Mississippi, as much as we give up here, they say. Money every year for twenty years. Goods. Blankets. A payment for the traders our people owe. And the promise that we go west within three years. Billy Caldwell and Alexander Robinson and the other chiefs signed for the united bands two summers ago.

Ask a man who has lost his country if a price was fair. The Americans would have taken it anyway. That is what the chiefs said: take what you can get, while you can get it. Some of our people say Caldwell sold us. Others say he saved what could be saved. Go and ask him. He will tell you his side.

This autumn or next spring. My father's grave is on the Des Plaines. My wife's mother is buried by the lake. My son was born at the Calumet. I will take them with me in my mouth, as names, since I cannot take them any other way.

asks.q: Why are so many camps by the river?
a: People have come from all the villages for the payment, for the money and the goods the treaty promised. They say it will be soon. We have been waiting a long time. While we wait, the whiskey sellers come to the camps every night, and the traders come with their books to say what everybody owes.

More than they ever had, by the traders' books. Every trader in Chicago has a claim, and the claims are paid out of our money before we see it. A man may come away from the payment with a blanket and a hangover and nothing in his hand. That is how it was at the last one.

asks.q: What do you think of the town?
a: When I was young there were the fort, the Kinzie house, the Ouilmette house, a few French cabins and a great deal of grass. Now there are houses as far as you can see, and noise, and every man walking very fast. The river is full of boats. The prairie is full of men with chains measuring it.

The lake. The lake does not care. It was here when the Miami had this country and it will be here when the Americans have gone. In the morning I go down to the shore and look at it, and for a while the town behind me is quiet.

asks.q: Is there a chief who is a friend to the settlers?
a: Shabbona, of the Ottawa and Potawatomi, from the Fox River country. In the Black Hawk war he rode through the settlements day and night to warn the settlers that Black Hawk's men were coming, and many lived because of him. Some of our own people have never forgiven him.

He thought so. He had fought beside Tecumseh once, and he had seen what war against the Americans brought. He chose the settlers' lives over Black Hawk's war. A man can be right and still lose his friends. Shabbona knows that better than anyone.

asks.q: Will you take your horses west?
a: Every one. A man without a horse in that country is a man who walks behind other men. I have three: a mare for my wife, a strong one for the packs, and my own, who is fast and does not like Americans. He bit a trader last week. I was very proud of him.

more.q: What's the country like out west?
a: I have not seen it. Some went to look last year and came back saying it is grass with no trees and no sugar maples and the Sioux and the Osage close by. Some say it is good land. They always say the next land is good land.

asks.q: What do you sell in town?
a: Baskets of ash splint and sweetgrass, mats, moccasins with beadwork, maple sugar in birch-bark cones, berries in the season. The town women buy them and pay with flour or cloth or a few coins. Some of them are kind. Some of them count the coins twice before they give them.

Not by itself. With the hunting and the corn and the payment, yes, barely. When we go west there will be no town to sell to for a long while. I am making as many mats as I can, to take with us. A lodge needs mats wherever it stands.

asks.q: Do your children go to the town school?
a: My daughter went for a while, to the little school by the church, to learn the Americans' letters. She can write her name and read a little. The other girls stared at her. The teacher was kind. I wanted her to be able to read the papers the Americans make us sign.
In the west, who will teach her? I will ask her to teach her brothers. A people who can read the treaty can argue with it. That is something.

asks.q: Do you like coming to town?
a: The town is loud and smells bad and has too many people. But there are things to see: the boats, the soldiers drilling, the horses, the store with the shiny things in the window. The boys throw things at us sometimes. Sometimes they share their candy.

more.q: What's your favourite thing in town?
a: The bridge that goes up. We watched it go up for a boat and everybody on both sides was shouting. My brother says it is a trick. I think it is the best thing in the town.

asks.q: Are you going on a journey?
a: My mother says we are going far, across a big river, to a new place. We will walk and ride for many days. I asked if my dog can come. She said yes. Then I asked if the lake can come. She did not answer.
I do not know. My grandmother is sad. My father is quiet. My cousins say it will be an adventure. I will be sad if there are no strawberries.

asks.q: Which world do you belong to?
a: Both, and so neither, completely. My father was French, my mother Potawatomi. I can sit in council with the chiefs and at table with the agent. The treaty made a list of people like me, the mixed bloods, and gave us money and reservations of our own. Some people in the camps say that was our price.

Stay. I have a house and a reservation and a trade. Alexander Robinson is staying on his land on the Des Plaines, and he signed the treaty, and his people still come to his door. Go and ask him how it feels to stay when your relatives are going. He will tell you honestly. It will not make you feel better.

asks.q: Were you a voyageur?
a: Twenty years with the brigades, from Mackinac to the Illinois, paddling and carrying and singing. A voyageur's back is gone at forty, but his voice is the last thing to go. Now I work for Colonel Beaubien and sing in the evenings outside his door.

Jean Baptiste Beaubien, a militia colonel and the oldest trader in the town, after the Kinzies. He has two families and twenty children and the whole fort reservation, if the government lets him keep it. He is the most generous man in Chicago and the noisiest. Go and see him. He will kiss you on both cheeks.

asks.q: Are there many French families left?
a: The Beaubiens, the Laframboises, the Ouilmettes, the Mirandeaus, a few more. Before the Yankees came we were the town. Now we are the old part of the town. They cannot say our names and they buy our land at prices that make us laugh, and then they sell it at prices that make us cry.

I mind that they think nothing was here before them. My grandfather had a cabin by the river when this was a portage and a few lodges. The Yankees call it a wilderness. It was full of people. They were just not Yankees.

asks.q: What are you singing?
a: À la claire fontaine, the song every Frenchman on these rivers knows. My father sang it paddling. His father sang it paddling. I sing it now with a hammer. It is about a man who has lost his love for a rose he did not give her. All our songs are about love, even the ones about work.

more.q: Can you sing it in English?
a: Ha! It does not go into English. The English is all corners. In French it is round, like water. Listen to it once in French and you will understand it without the words.

asks.q: What did you think when you first saw Chicago?
a: I cried. I will not pretend otherwise. We came in on the schooner in a grey rain and there was the fort, and a few dozen houses, and mud as far as the eye could see. My husband said it was the finest town in the West. I asked him where it was.

I like the people. Every woman in this town came from somewhere else and left somebody behind, so we look after each other. Mrs. Kinzie, the agent's wife, came out in thirty-one and wrote home that it was a wilderness, and now she gives the best suppers in Chicago. Go and see her. She will tell you how she crossed the prairie in winter on horseback.

My mother's garden in Connecticut. Apple trees. A paved street. A church with a bell. A shop with a proper ribbon counter. Silence. You cannot get any silence here: hammers all day and fiddles all night.

asks.q: How much does it cost to keep house here?
a: Everything comes on a boat and the boat sets the price. Flour twelve dollars the barrel this spring, when the boats were late; eggs dear; butter dearer, and half of it rancid by the time it gets here. A woman with a cow and a hen yard is a rich woman, whatever her husband is.

Calico, tea, sugar, candles, pins, and whatever the store has that it did not have last week. Mr. Gale has books and paper and, once, a parcel of Boston magazines that every lady in town read in a single week and passed round until they fell apart. Everybody watches the landing for the next lot.

asks.q: How do you do the washing here?
a: Carry the water from the river or the lake, heat it in a copper over the fire, scrub on a board with soft soap, rinse, wring, and hang it out where the mud will not splash it, which is nowhere. Monday is wash day. Monday is also when everybody's husband brings home the mud of a week.

Clean enough for washing if you take it from the lake, not the river. The river has the slaughterhouse and the tannery in it, and everything from the town. A girl who boils the river water for drinking is wiser than one who does not.

asks.q: Is there much society here?
a: More than you would think. There are sewing circles at the churches, a ladies' society for the poor, suppers at the Kinzies', a ball now and then at the Tremont or the Sauganash. In winter, sleigh rides on the river ice and on the prairie. A girl can dance until two in this town and be up to milk the cow at five.

Mrs. Kinzie, for the old families. The ministers' wives, for the churches. Mrs. Porter, who was Miss Chappel and ran the school until she married the minister last month. She has more friends than anyone and fewer enemies.

asks.q: What does your husband do?
a: Whatever pays, this year. He came as a carpenter, then he was a clerk, then he took a contract on the harbour, and now he is in land. I married a carpenter. I am not sure what I have now. He comes home talking about lots on Wolf Point and Wabash Avenue as if they were cows we owned.
I keep a little money of my own in a stocking in the flour barrel, in silver. If the land goes up I will spend it on a new dress. If it goes down I will spend it on bread. Either way I sleep better.

asks.q: What do you do when your children are sick?
a: Pray, and send for the doctor if we can pay him, and if we cannot, ask a neighbour. There are good doctors here now: Kimberly, Egan, Maxwell at the fort. For ague, quinine; for a cough, a mustard plaster; for the summer flux, boiled water and arrowroot and a great deal of sitting up at night.

A baby, in our first summer. Most women here have. We put the little ones in the ground on the lake shore and then on the new burying ground and we go home and cook supper. That is what a woman does. You do not stop.

asks.q: Is it hard to find a servant here?
a: The hardest thing in Chicago. A good girl comes off the boat in the morning and by night she has three offers of marriage and a better position. We pay twice what they pay in New York, and still they leave. My Irish girl is the fourth this year, and I would sooner lose my husband than her.

Ireland, mostly, by Quebec or New York, and some Yankee farm girls from the East, and a few from the old French families. Mary Flynn is the best girl in town. She keeps a family's silver as if it were her own. Go and ask her how she likes it here. She may tell you more than she tells her mistress.

asks.q: Where do ladies get their dresses?
a: From the dressmakers in town, of whom there are now three or four, and the best is a French girl, Archange Laframboise, whose family has been here since before the soldiers. She makes over the New York fashions from the magazines, with sleeves as big as hams. You cannot go through a door sideways in them.

Not at all. A lady in Chicago lifts her skirts six inches at every crossing and loses a slipper in the mud every week. But she will not be outdressed by a lady in Detroit. Miss Laframboise will measure you before you can say no.

asks.q: How's business for a dressmaker?
a: More than I can do. Every boat brings ladies who need gowns let out from the journey, and widows who need mourning, and brides who need everything at once. I sew from six in the morning till the candle gives out. My fingers are like a pincushion.

The land men's wives. A man makes a thousand dollars on a lot and his wife wants a silk the same week. I sew silk for the rich and calico for the rest and mend for everybody. Whatever the town is doing, it shows up first in the sleeves.

asks.q: How many people live in your house?
a: Twenty-two this week, and nine more on the floor when the boat came in Tuesday. I cook three meals a day for all of them, with one girl to help and my husband to carry the water. They pay two dollars a week, when they pay. Some of them leave in the night with their bags out the window.

Pork, potatoes, bread, beans, coffee and pie. Fish when the boys catch it. Whatever is cheap at the landing that morning. They complain, and they come back for more, and they tell their friends. A full table is the best advertisement.
A gentleman who says he is a poet and pays in verses. I have accepted two. They were not very good. He is behind four weeks now, and I have stopped reading them.

asks.q: Do you like your work?
a: It is work. I rise at five, light the fires, carry water, cook breakfast for the family, wash, scrub, iron, cook dinner, mend, cook supper, wash up, and go to bed in the little room behind the kitchen. On Sunday afternoon I walk out. On Thursday evening I may go to Mass.

Until I marry, and a girl here can marry any week she likes. Mary Flynn says she will stay with her mistress because her mistress trusts her with the silver. I say a girl should trust herself first. Go and ask Mary. We disagree about everything, and we are best friends.

asks.q: Where's home for you?
a: Galway, by way of Quebec and a summer in Buffalo. My brothers are on the canals in New York. My mother is still in the cottage with the little ones. I send her a dollar in every letter. The postmaster knows my writing by now.

I miss the sea and the singing and the Sundays. Here the Mass is in a little wooden church, Saint Mary's, and the priest is French, Father St. Cyr, and half the people are French. But the prayers are the same, and that is something. Go and hear him say Mass. He has a lovely voice, though his English makes us laugh.
If the right man asks. There are ten men in this town for every girl, so the asking is not the trouble. The choosing is.

asks.q: Whose washing do you take in?
a: The fort's, some of it, and the Tremont's sheets, and a few gentlemen's shirts. I have a copper, two tubs, a board, a mangle I bought with my first year's money and a line strung right across the yard. On a good drying day I can do six baskets.

Better than service, because I am my own mistress. Worse for the hands. Look at them. The lye eats the skin and the cold water cracks it, and in the winter they bleed. But nobody tells me when to get up, except the washing.

asks.q: How many pupils do you have?
a: Thirty or forty in the winter, when there is nothing else for the children to do, and a dozen in the summer, when there is everything. Ages five to fifteen, in one room, on benches, with slates and whatever books their parents brought with them. I teach the alphabet in one corner and fractions in the other at the same time.

more.q: Who was the first teacher here?
a: Mr. Watkins, in thirty-two, in a little log room, with a dozen scholars, half of them French. Then Miss Chappel, who married Mr. Porter. Now there are schools all over town. Go and ask Mr. Watkins what the first day was like. He says the children taught him more than he taught them.

Keeping the boys in school when a boat comes in. They hear the whistle and they are gone, out the window and down to the landing to carry bags for pennies. I have learned to stop the lesson and go with them. We do our arithmetic on the bags.

asks.q: What do girls do for fun here?
a: Walk out on the lake shore on a Sunday afternoon in our best bonnets and pretend not to look at the officers from the fort. Pick strawberries on the prairie in June. Go to the singing school at the church on Thursday. In winter, skate on the river, and sleigh, and dance until the fiddler falls asleep.

I am not telling you! He is a clerk at a store on Lake Street, and he has red hair, and that is all you will get out of me. My mother says he has no prospects. Every clerk in this town has prospects. That is what this town is for.

asks.q: What's the most exciting thing that's happened here?
a: When the Potawatomi danced through town at the treaty, painted and singing, going down Lake Street and past the houses, and everybody standing in the doorways not sure whether to be afraid. That was a story they still tell about two summers ago, at the treaty. People say there will be another when the payment comes.

I was at the treaty, two years ago, when I was small, and I remember all the people camped round the town, thousands, and the smoke, and the horses. My father said it was the last time we would see them like that. Go down by the river and look. Some of them are here now.

asks.q: Is there music in town?
a: Every night, somewhere. Mark Beaubien plays the fiddle at the Sauganash and anybody who can dance does. There is a singing school at the Presbyterian church for the hymns. The soldiers at the fort have a drummer and a fifer. And the French families sing old songs at their doors in the evening that nobody else understands.

A reel at the Sauganash, when Mark is in the mood and the floor is full and somebody's husband has to hold the candles because there is no room for a table. They say he never plays the same tune twice. They say he never stops till the last guest falls down.

asks.q: Have you ever got stuck in the mud?
a: Every day! Yesterday I lost a shoe on Clark Street. It is still there. My brother says someday they will dig it up and put it in a museum. Once a pig got stuck in front of our house and the whole street came out to watch.

more.q: Did they get the pig out?
a: Three men and a plank and a rope. The pig got out and the men fell in. My mother said not to laugh. I laughed until I fell down. Then I was stuck too.

asks.q: Do you watch the boats come in?
a: When the bell goes or somebody shouts sail, everybody runs to the river. I can tell the schooners apart by their sails. When a steamboat comes, it blows smoke and has a big wheel on the side that splashes, and all the dogs bark.

People, mostly, with trunks and babies and bundles, looking at the mud. And barrels and boxes and a piano once. They carried it up the street on poles and a lady played it right there on the landing. Everybody clapped.

asks.q: Do you go to school?
a: I did, to Miss Chappel, but now she is Mrs. Porter and she is married so she is not my teacher any more. Now I go to a man who smells of tobacco and has a stick. I miss Miss Chappel. She gave us a ribbon if we said our lessons right.
My letters, and to count to a hundred, and the names of the states, and a hymn. And that the earth goes round the sun. My grandfather does not believe it. He says he would feel it.

asks.q: Do you know any Potawatomi children?
a: Some come with their mothers to sell berries and baskets. One girl showed me how to make a doll from corn husks. We could not talk, so we did it with our hands. Then her mother called her and they went back to the camp by the river.
My father says they have to go west across the big river because of the treaty. I asked why. He said because the government says so. I asked why again and he said go and play. So I am asking you.

asks.q: Do you have any pets?
a: A cat, a dog, a pig that is not supposed to be a pet but is, and a crow that my brother found with a broken wing. The crow says one word. It sounds like Mother. My mother does not think that is funny.
Andrew Jackson. My father named him. My mother says it is not respectful. My father says the pig does not mind.

asks.q: Have you been inside the fort?
a: Once, with my father, to see the soldiers drill. They all move at the same time like one big animal. There is a cannon on the blockhouse and when they fire it at sunset everything shakes and the birds all fly up.

The major. He has a sword and a horse and he does not smile. My father says he is a good man really. My father says the fort will go soon, because the town does not need protecting any more. I asked from what. He did not say.

asks.q: What's the best thing to eat here?
a: Wild strawberries on the prairie in June, so many your hands go red. And plums in the fall. And maple sugar from the Potawatomi in spring. And fish my father catches off the pier. And the pie at the Sauganash, but only once, because it costs too much.

more.q: Where do you find the strawberries?
a: Out past the last houses on the prairie, where the grass is low. You lie down on your stomach and eat them right off the plant. My mother sends us with a pail and we come home with a pail half full and our stomachs very full.

asks.q: Do you speak French?
a: My grandmother speaks only French and Potawatomi, and my father French and English, and I speak all three, but my English is best because of school. At home we say grace in French. At school I am not allowed to.
Bonjour. That is hello. And bouette, that is mud, the way my grandmother says it, and it is the most important word in Chicago. She says it ten times a day when we come in.

asks.q: Have you seen a wolf?
a: I heard one! At night, from our house at the edge of town. It went ow-ow-oooo and then another one answered. My mother shut the window. My brother said it was coming to eat me. I hit him. Then I could not sleep.

In the daytime, far away on the prairie, a grey thing running. My father said it was a prairie wolf and it was more afraid of us than we were of it. I do not think he is right. It did not look afraid.

asks.q: Do you like the boats?
a: Boat! Big boat. It goes toot. I was on a boat. A long time. I was sick.
From far. From grandma. She is not here. She is on the other side of the water.

asks.q: Why are you so muddy?
a: I was jumping. In the big puddle. Splash! My mother is cross.
Yes! I want to do it again. Do not tell.

asks.q: Is that your dog?
a: He is mine. He licks my face. He is big. Bigger than me.
Bowser. No, Rowser. No. I do not know. He is Dog.

asks.q: Do you hear the bell?
a: Ding ding! At church. It is loud. I put my hands on my ears.
I go. I sit. I have to be quiet. It is hard.

asks.q: What's your favourite thing?
a: Cake. And my blanket. And Papa. Papa is first. Then cake.
No. Tomorrow. It is a birthday. Not mine. But I can have some.

asks.q: Can you count?
a: One, two, five, ten! I can count cats. One cat. Another cat. Two cats.

more.q: How many cats do you have?
a: One. But she is going to have more. My mother says. In the box.

asks.q: Are you ready for the Fourth of July?
a: Three days to go and I have four pies to bake and a dress to let out. There will be a salute from the fort, a procession, the Declaration read out by a lawyer who will take an hour about it, and a dinner at the Tremont for the gentlemen. The ladies will watch from the windows, and then we shall all dance.

The fireworks, if the powder came on the last boat. Last year it did not, and the soldiers fired the cannon instead, twenty-four times, one for each state, and broke two windows on Water Street. Ask any soldier at the fort about it. They still laugh.

asks.q: Can anything grow in this mud?
a: Anything at all, if you can keep the pigs out of it. The ground is black and rich and you can put a seed in and stand back. My beans are over the fence already. My cabbages are the size of a baby's head. The trouble is the water: one wet week and the whole garden is a pond with lettuce floating in it.

Potatoes, beans, peas, onions, cabbages, squash and a row of flowers for my soul, hollyhocks and pinks. A woman needs something to look at that is not mud. The Potawatomi women showed me how to plant the beans by the corn so the corn holds them up. They know more about this ground than any of us.

asks.q: Do you write to your family back East?
a: Every week, to my sister in Vermont. I tell her about the town and the prices and the people and the mud, and she writes back that I must be exaggerating. I sent her a lock of mud once, wrapped in paper. She never mentioned it.

more.q: What do they think of Chicago?
a: They think I live among wolves and savages and gamblers. The wolves are real. The gamblers are real. The savages are mostly the Yankees on Saturday night. The Potawatomi women who sell me baskets have better manners than half the men at the land office.

asks.q: How old is your baby?
a: Six months, born in January in the coldest week of the winter, with the snow up to the window and the doctor stuck at the fort. My neighbour came across with a lantern and stayed till morning. That is how it is here. You have no family, so your neighbours become your family.

A French woman, a Laframboise, who has had seven children and knew exactly what to do. She speaks very little English and I speak no French, and we managed perfectly. She made me a broth that I would give a lot to taste again.

asks.q: Is that your cow wandering down the street?
a: She is, the wretch. She gets out every morning and goes to the river to drink, and then she stands in the middle of Lake Street and the teamsters have to go round her. The town has an ordinance against animals running loose. Nobody pays any mind to it, least of all the cow.
Mrs. Jackson, after the President's late wife, because my husband is a Whig and thinks it is funny. I do not. But she gives four quarts a day, and in this town a cow is worth more than a lot.

asks.q: Where did you get that bonnet?
a: From a milliner on Lake Street, who had it from New York in May. Straw, with a silk ribbon and a bunch of flowers made of cloth. It cost me three dollars and my husband nearly fainted. But a woman cannot walk out on the lake shore on a Sunday in last year's bonnet. Not here. Not now.

Everyone tries. The land men's wives have the silks and the French girls have the best taste, and the rest of us copy whoever walked past last. The fashions here are about three months behind New York and six months ahead of Detroit.

asks.q: What do the church ladies do?
a: Sew. We have a sewing circle every Wednesday at the minister's house and we make clothes for the poor, quilts for the church, and money for the bell we are saving for. We also talk a great deal about everybody who is not there, which is the real business of a sewing circle.

This week: whether the new doctor is married, why Mr. Ogden has stayed so long when he said he was going back to New York, and who has bought the lot next to the church. We know everything in this town a week before the newspapers.

asks.q: Are you on your own here?
a: I am a widow, since last autumn. My husband took the fever on a contract at the harbour and was gone in a week. I have two children and his tools and a lot on the South Side that he bought for fifty dollars and that a man offered me four hundred for in May.

Not yet. Everybody tells me to sell and everybody tells me to hold, and all of them want something. I take in sewing and boarders and I wait. A widow in this town finds out quickly which of her husband's friends were really his friends.

asks.q: What do you do on Sunday?
a: Church in the morning, dinner at noon, and in the afternoon everybody walks out along the lake shore by the fort, in their best clothes, to see and be seen. The young men pretend to look at the water. The young women pretend not to look at the young men. The old ladies look at everybody.

On a fine afternoon in June, with the lake blue and the sails out on it and the prairie flowers coming up through the grass behind the town, it is the prettiest place I have ever lived. Then you turn round and see Lake Street.

asks.q: What's that big building going up?
a: The Lake House, on the north side, brick, three storeys, with a dining room, they say, as grand as anything in New York. The men building it are Kinzie and his partners. It will not be finished till next year at this rate. When it is, they say they will serve oysters from Baltimore.
On my birthday, if my husband has made his money by then. If not, I will stand outside and smell the oysters. Either way, it is good for the town. A town with oysters is a city.

asks.q: Have you ever thought of deserting?
a: Every day, looking at Lake Street from the blockhouse. A carpenter there makes in a week what I make in a month. But I have two years left and a sergeant who watches me, and if they catch you they shave your head and drum you out and your name is in the paper. I would sooner leave by the gate with a discharge in my pocket.
More than the major likes to say. The town hides them: a man disappears at night and turns up on a roof somewhere with a different name and a hammer. Everybody knows. Nobody tells.

asks.q: Will you be guarding the payment?
a: When it comes, yes. All the Potawatomi from every village will be camped round the town and the money will come in kegs under guard. Our job is to stand between the money and the whiskey sellers and the claim men, and keep the peace. It is the only real work this fort will do this year.

Not from the Potawatomi. They are the most patient people I have ever seen. From the whiskey sellers and the traders with their books, yes, a little. They want the money before the people get it. We are supposed to stop that. Mostly we cannot.

asks.q: Is this the same fort as before the war?
a: No. The first Fort Dearborn was burned after the battle in 1812. The army came back in 1816 and built this one on nearly the same ground. Some of the logs are from the old one, they say, and the old soldiers swear that on a still night you can hear something on the shore where the battle was.
I have stood sentry on the south blockhouse at two in the morning with the wind off the lake and heard things I did not like. Probably the wind. Probably owls. I did not go down to look.

asks.q: Who does the cooking at the fort?
a: We take turns, by mess, eight men to a mess, and one of us cooks each week. Salt pork, beans, bread from the fort's oven, beef when the contractor brings it, fish when we catch it. On my week the men complain. On the Irishman's week they eat everything and ask for more.
Onions, and a bit of whatever he can trade for in town. He goes over the wall at night for herbs, he says. I do not ask what else he goes over the wall for.

asks.q: Why is there so much whiskey in the camps?
a: Because the traders bring it, at night, in barrels on carts, and sell it for anything: a blanket, a gun, a horse, the promise of the payment money. The young men drink it to forget, and the old men drink it because the young men do, and the women hide the knives.

The agent tries. The soldiers try. The chiefs try. But the whiskey sellers are clever and the town is full of them, and every man of them has a claim against the payment. Some of our people do not drink at all, and they are the ones who will get to the west country with their horses.

asks.q: Do you speak English?
a: A little, for trade. Yes, no, how much, too much, whiskey, God damn. That is what the Americans teach us. My son speaks more, from the town. He says words I do not know, and laughs when I say them back wrong.

more.q: Will your language survive in the west?
a: As long as there are mothers to speak it to children. Our language has crossed lakes and rivers before. It will cross the Mississippi. What it will lose is the names of this place: the river, the lake, the wild leek, the portage. Words for a place die when nobody stands in it.

asks.q: What will you leave behind?
a: My mother's grave, on a rise by the Des Plaines, with a little house of bark over it. I visit her every spring with tobacco and food. When we go west, nobody will visit her. The Americans will plough the rise. That is the hardest thing.

more.q: Can you take anything of hers?
a: Her kettle, her awl, a belt she wove, and her stories, which I have told to my daughter. That is all a woman leaves anyway. The rest goes back to the ground, wherever the ground is.

asks.q: How did you find your place?
a: I stood on the landing with my bundle the day the boat came in, and a lady came down from the street and looked at my hands and asked could I cook. I said I could. That was a lie, but I learned by Friday. She has kept me a year now and raised my wages twice.

She is fair, which is more than kind. She pays on the day and she does not count the sugar. She has a temper when the mud comes in on the floor, but so would anyone. When I marry, I will ask her to stand up for me. She will cry. She cries at everything.

asks.q: Why is everyone in such a hurry?
a: Because the land office opened this spring and the government is selling the country round here at a dollar and a quarter an acre, and lots in town that went for a hundred dollars three years ago are going for thousands. Every boat brings a hundred more men off the lake with money in their boots and the same idea in their heads.

Some of it. Some of it is paper from banks in Michigan that may or may not be there next year. A man buys a lot on Lake Street for a note, sells it the same afternoon for a bigger note, and goes to supper rich. Mr. Ogden came from New York last month to sell his brother-in-law's land and found it worth ten times what they paid. Go and ask him if he believes it yet.
A forty out on the prairie and a quarter-lot off Clark Street, on credit. My wife thinks I am mad. If the canal comes, I am a rich man. If it does not, I have a lot of very wet grass.

asks.q: Is the mud always this bad?
a: This is a dry week. In April a team of oxen went down on Lake Street up to the yoke and they had to dig it out with planks. Somebody put up a sign in the slough at Clark Street: No Bottom Here. Somebody else stuck an old hat on a stick in the middle of the street with a board beside it: The Shortest Road to China.

Drain it where? The whole town is about four feet above the lake on a good day. Rain comes and has nowhere to go. They talk about raising the streets, one day, when the town is rich. I say they had better raise the people first.
Boots to the knee and a plank to stand on. And never wear your good trousers on a Tuesday. Tuesday is when the teamsters come in.

asks.q: What canal does everyone keep talking about?
a: The Illinois and Michigan canal: a ditch from the South Branch over the old portage to the Des Plaines and down to the Illinois River, so a boat can go from the lakes to the Mississippi without anybody carrying it. The French talked about it a hundred and fifty years ago. The state passed a law this winter to borrow the money for it.

Next year, they say, or the year after. Every year they say next year. But this time the state has the land from Congress and the commissioners are laying out the line. When the digging starts there will be work for a thousand men, and every one of them will need boots and bread and whiskey. Mr. Hubbard is a canal man. Ask him how deep it will be. He will draw it for you in the dust.

asks.q: How did you get to Chicago?
a: By steamboat from Buffalo to Detroit, and by schooner round the top of Michigan to here, two weeks and a half with forty people sleeping on the deck and the cook drunk from Mackinac on. When we came in there was no harbour, only a sandbar across the river mouth, and they rowed us ashore in a lighter and dropped us in the lake up to our knees.

The government is building one. Two long piers going out into the lake, and last year the spring flood cut a channel straight through the bar and the schooners can come right up into the river now. Lieutenant Allen of the army is in charge of the work. Go and look at his piers. They are the best thing in Chicago.

asks.q: Do people get sick here?
a: Every summer. Fever and ague: you shake till your teeth chatter, then you burn, then you are well for a day, then it comes again. They say it comes off the marshes. Half the men in this town have been yellow at some time. They take quinine and whiskey and go back to work.

That was in thirty-two, when General Scott's soldiers came through for the Black Hawk war. They brought it on the boats and it went through the fort like a scythe. People still do not like to talk about it. They buried the dead on the lake shore and moved on.

asks.q: Are there wolves out there?
a: On the prairie past the last houses, yes, prairie wolves, and you hear them most nights. Last winter the town turned out for a wolf hunt: men on horseback in a great ring, closing in, with dogs and guns and a lot of shouting. They got a few. They got more of each other's toes.

After the garbage. A wolf came right up behind the Sauganash in February and took a goose off the woodpile. Mark Beaubien fired at it with his fiddle in the other hand. He missed. He says it was the fiddle's fault.

asks.q: What brought you across the water?
a: Hunger, mostly. Four of us on half an acre in County Cork, and the rent going up and the potatoes going black. I worked my passage to Quebec and walked to the States and followed the work: a canal in New York, a road in Ohio, and now Chicago, where they say there will be a canal that will need ten thousand of us.

A dollar a day for a man with a shovel, when there is work, and nobody to touch his cap to. Better, yes. The Yankees look at you as if you smelled, but the money is the same colour in an Irishman's pocket. Patrick Mahoney came the same road I did, and he has the luck of the devil. Ask him about the hay wagon.

Saint Mary's, the little Catholic church on Lake Street, with Father St. Cyr. Wood and nails and not much of either. On a Sunday you hear Irish and French and Potawatomi and a bit of German, all saying the same prayers in different voices.

asks.q: What work are you doing?
a: Harbour work for the government: driving piles, filling cribs with stone, building the north pier out into the lake. It is cold work even in July. The lake comes in green over the cribs and you are wet to the waist from seven until six.

Lieutenant Allen, a young engineer from the army. He knows his business. He is up on the pier at sunrise looking at the sand, because the sand is the enemy: it drifts in along the shore and fills the channel, and he has to keep it out. Go and ask him about it. He talks about sand the way other men talk about women.

asks.q: Where do you sleep?
a: In a boarding house on Lake Street, eight to a room and two to a bed, for two dollars a week with meals. The landlady counts the potatoes. The man I share with snores and the man in the next bed sings in his sleep. When a boat comes in, they put more men on the floor.

Not until you build it. Every house in Chicago has a family downstairs and boarders up the ladder. They put up frame houses in a week, now, with these new light frames of sawn studs nailed together, no posts and beams at all. The old carpenters say they will blow away. So far they have not.

asks.q: How do they build houses so fast here?
a: A new way of framing, with thin sawn studs and joists, two by fours and two by sixes, nailed together instead of mortised and pegged. Four men can put up the frame of a house in a day or two. Carpenters from back East laugh at them and say a good wind will carry them off. This town has no time for the old way.

People argue. Some say Mr. Taylor, the carpenter who built Saint Mary's. Some say the idea came from all over and nobody owns it. The nails are what make it possible: cut nails, cheap, by the keg. Mr. Peck built the first frame store, on South Water Street. Go and ask him what he paid for his nails.

asks.q: What's your trade?
a: Blacksmith, at the forge on Lake Street. Shoeing horses and oxen, mending wagon tyres, making hinges, nails, chain, ploughshares, and whatever else a new country needs. The teamsters bring me broken things all day long. On a good day I hear the anvil in my sleep.

more.q: Is it a good trade here?
a: The best. Everyone needs iron and nobody can wait for it to come from Buffalo. I came with my tools and a hundred dollars. I have three men working for me now and a house with a floor. My father would not believe it.

A prairie plough. The prairie sod is so thick with roots that an ordinary plough breaks on it. You need a breaking plough with a long iron share, filed sharp, and six yoke of oxen to pull it. The first breaking is the hardest work there is. After that, the black ground just opens.

asks.q: What do you make all day?
a: Barrels. Pork barrels, beef barrels, flour barrels, whiskey barrels, fish barrels. Mr. Dole and Mr. Hubbard pack pork and beef every autumn, and every pound of it goes east in a barrel I made or a man like me made. Oak staves, iron hoops, and a good tight head.

Seven years an apprentice in Vermont. The trick is the bend: you heat the staves over a fire and pull them in with a windlass till they make the shape. Too hot and they crack, too cold and they will not bend. I can tell by the smell.

asks.q: Are clothes expensive here?
a: Everything is expensive here. Broadcloth comes from New York by lake and costs twice what it does there. A gentleman's coat from me is eighteen dollars and he will need a new one every year, because the mud eats the bottoms of everything. The land men all want to look rich, and the rich all want to look like land men.

The lawyers. There are more lawyers in this town every week, and every one of them wants a black coat that looks as if it has been to Washington. Young Caton is a good customer. He pays on time, which is rarer than a good coat.

asks.q: What do you sell?
a: Dry goods, groceries, hardware, crockery, books, boots, whatever came off the last schooner. A man comes in for a plough and goes out with a plough, a bonnet for his wife, a pound of tea, a set of plates and a Bible. Half my customers pay in cash and half pay in promises.

From New York, by the Erie Canal to Buffalo and by lake to here. It takes a month if the weather is good and two if it is not. I order in the spring for the autumn and pray the boat does not go down. Mr. Gale has the bookshop on Lake Street. He gets the newspapers first. He knows the New York prices before anybody.

Business is so good it frightens me. Everybody is buying everything. When a whole town is buying and nobody is making, somebody is going to be sorry. I keep my own money in gold. Do not tell my partner.

asks.q: Is there still a fur trade here?
a: What is left of it. The American Fur Company still sends goods to the Potawatomi and takes their furs, but the furs are thinner every year and the people are being moved west. The old traders like Mr. Hubbard have gone into pork and land and warehouses. The fur trade is a dead man still walking.

The beaver are gone from the near rivers. The muskrat are being drained out with the marshes. The Potawatomi signed their land away two years ago and are going across the Mississippi. A fur trade needs wild country and the people who live in it. This is a town now.

asks.q: Is there much law in Chicago?
a: More every day. Land titles, mostly: a lot sold four times in a week by men who never saw it, and then two of them turn up on the same morning with deeds. I could fill my office with land cases and never see a thief or a murderer.

Young Caton is clever and hungry. Mr. Hamilton holds every office in the county and is the most useful man to know. There are new men from New York every week with letters of introduction and no clients. Go and see Caton. He will tell you how he won his first case, which is a story he likes very much.

asks.q: What's the most common complaint you treat?
a: Fever and ague, as everybody calls it. A man shakes in the morning and burns in the afternoon and is weak as a kitten for a week. Quinine is the cure, if the patient can afford it. Next are broken bones, from wagons and timber and the mud, and after that drink.
