Too many and too few that pay. Doctor Kimberly and Doctor Egan have the best practices. Kimberly has been here since thirty-two and has seen the cholera. Go and ask him about it if you have a strong stomach.

asks.q: Which newspaper do you read?
a: Both of them, now. The Democrat, which Mr. Calhoun has printed since thirty-three, and the American, which Mr. Davis started this June. One is for Jackson and one is against him. Between them you get the truth, if you read the one and then the other and believe neither.

The best entertainment in town. Each says the other is the mouthpiece of a ring of land men, and both are probably right. The town reads them aloud in the taverns and cheers the insults. Go and find Mr. Davis. Ask him what Mr. Calhoun called him this week.

asks.q: What do you do for the store?
a: Everything the owner does not want to. I open at six and sweep out the mud, weigh out sugar and tea and nails, measure calico, write up the accounts, chase the debts and sleep under the counter to guard the stock. Eight dollars a month and my keep.

more.q: Do you want to own a store?
a: Every clerk in this town wants to own something. Young Wright clerked when he came and now he is buying lots and talking about schools and newspapers as if he owned the place. Go and ask him how he did it. He will tell you it was hard work. It was also his father's money. Both are true.

asks.q: Is your house full?
a: Full is not the word. Every bed, every floor, every table after supper is pushed together and three men sleep on it. A boat came in yesterday with sixty people and I fed all of them. My wife cooked until midnight.

The Tremont, the Couch brothers' place at Lake and Dearborn, is the newest and the grandest, with real beds. The Sauganash is the merriest, because Mark Beaubien plays the fiddle and dances with the guests. I keep the cleanest, though nobody gives me any credit for it. Go and see Ira Couch. He will show you his new bedsteads as if they were his children.

asks.q: What do you do all day?
a: Errands for Mr. Wright's store: carry a letter to the post office, run a parcel to the landing, fetch the boss's dinner from the Sauganash. Sometimes I hold a horse while a gentleman goes in somewhere. A penny for that. When the boats come in, I carry bags. Two pennies a bag.

In the winter, a bit. In summer there is too much money to be made. Miss Chappel had a school in a room off the church. She married the minister this summer, Mr. Porter. Go and ask her if she remembers me. She does. I put a frog in her desk.

more.q: What do you want to be?
a: Rich. Like everybody here. Or a steamboat captain. Or both. A steamboat captain who owns the steamboat.

asks.q: Have you crossed the new bridge?
a: The drawbridge at Dearborn Street? Everybody has. It goes up in the middle so the schooners can get through, and when it is up everybody stands on both sides shouting at each other. Last week a man was so busy shouting he walked his horse into the river.

Before last year there was only a ferry, and before that a canoe. Mark Beaubien used to row people across for a few pennies, and he still says the river was better before. He says the bridge ruined a perfectly good business. Go and ask him. He will play you a tune about it.

asks.q: What's all the shouting down the street?
a: The auctioneers, selling lots. A man stands on a barrel outside the land office or on the porch of a tavern with a map and a hammer, and sells a piece of ground that half the bidders have never seen and the other half could not find. Going, going, gone, and somebody has bought a piece of wet prairie for five hundred dollars.

more.q: Do the buyers ever see the land?
a: Some ride out to look. Some do not bother; they will sell it next week to somebody else who will not see it either. Mr. Newberry bought land on the north side years ago, when it was nothing. Ask him what it was worth then and what it is worth now. Then sit down.

asks.q: Who's in charge of this town?
a: The board of trustees, five men elected each year, since the town was incorporated two summers ago. They pass ordinances about pigs in the streets and fires and the market, and nobody pays them any mind until somebody's pig eats somebody's cabbages. Then there is a meeting.

I am for Chicago. Jackson's men are the ones who hold the land office and the post office, so most of the town is for Jackson at least until the lots are paid for. The Whigs say the President is a tyrant. The Democrats say the Whigs are bankers. Both are partly right.

asks.q: Where are those wagons going?
a: West, to the Fox River and the Rock River and Galena, with goods, and coming back with lead and grain. Every day a dozen teams go out on the Ottawa road and a dozen come in. I drive one of them, four yoke of oxen and a wagon full of salt and iron and whiskey. Three days to the Fox, if it does not rain.

There is no road. There is a line of ruts across the prairie, and when the ruts get too deep we drive beside them and make new ones. In spring the sloughs are axle deep and you unload, carry the goods across, drag the wagon through empty and load again.

asks.q: Where does the meat come from?
a: Cattle are driven in from the prairie and from as far as Indiana and Ohio. Mr. Clybourne has the slaughterhouse up the North Branch and sells beef to the fort and the town. In the autumn they kill hogs by the thousand and pack them in salt in barrels for the boats east.

The best in Chicago after land, and land does not smell as bad. A man who can feed a town of three thousand that has no farms of its own will never be poor. Go and see Mr. Clybourne. He started selling beef to the soldiers before there was a town at all.

asks.q: What do men do at night here?
a: Drink, play cards, argue about land, and drink. There are more taverns than churches and more card tables than both. On a Saturday night you can hear the fiddles from three houses at once, and a fight starts somewhere about eleven and finishes about half past.

There is a debating society that meets at the Lyceum and argues about whether the canal or the railroad is the future. There is a temperance society that meets on the same night, and loses members to the debating society, which serves punch. And there is the church, for those who are tired of the rest.

asks.q: Are there farms around here?
a: A few, out along the North Branch and the Des Plaines and south towards the Calumet. The ground is the richest I have ever seen, black and deep, but it is so wet in spring and so hard to break that most men here would rather buy and sell it than plough it.

more.q: Will they farm it one day?
a: When the canal is dug and the land is drained and the price comes down, maybe. Right now a man can make more money selling a field in an afternoon than growing corn on it in five years. That is the trouble with this town in one sentence.

asks.q: What happens if a house catches fire?
a: Everybody runs with buckets. There is no engine yet, and no company, only a law that every householder must keep two leather buckets and turn out when the alarm is given. The houses are all wood and close together and the wind off the prairie is strong. One bad night and the whole town could go.

Not yet. Small fires, a chimney here and a shed there. But every winter somebody's stovepipe sets a roof going and the whole street forms a line from the river. One day they will need more than buckets. Most men here would rather not think about it.

asks.q: How do you get news from home?
a: From Mr. Hogan's post office, which is a room behind his store. The mail comes overland from Detroit or round by the lake, once or twice a week if the roads are open. When it comes in, half the town is at the door, and he calls the names out like a schoolmaster.

To my mother, every month. It costs twenty-five cents to send a letter that far, and she has to pay to receive it, so I write small and fill the page both ways. I tell her the town is a fine town. I do not tell her about the mud. Go and see Mr. Hogan. He knows everybody's business by the handwriting on their letters.

asks.q: What's that terrible smell?
a: The tannery, up the river. Hides soaking in lime and bark and worse in big pits, for weeks. They make leather for boots and harness and belts. A town of horses and oxen needs a lot of leather. A town of noses would rather it were made somewhere else.

Mr. Miller, up on the North Branch, has one, and Mr. Hall has another. Good men, but nobody sits next to them in church. Go and see Mr. Miller if you can stand it. He will tell you that a man stops smelling it after a week. His wife says otherwise.

asks.q: Whose church is that?
a: That one is the Presbyterians', built two years ago, and the minister is Mr. Porter, who came with the soldiers from the Sault two summers ago. The Baptists meet down by the fort, the Methodists in a house, and the Catholics have Saint Mary's. The Episcopalians are building. Everyone has a church in Chicago except the people who most need one.
When it rains. When it is fine I go and look at lots. My wife says I have the worship of the wrong thing. She may be right.

asks.q: What do you think of the President?
a: Old Hickory? He beat the British at New Orleans and the Bank in Washington, and he says the common man ought to have his say. Most of us here are common men, so most of us like him. He also wants every Indian east of the Mississippi moved west, and that has made a good deal of the land here available. Some men are glad of it. Some are quieter about it.
Until next year's election, and then his man Van Buren, they say. The Whigs here hate him. The Democrats here hold all the government posts. In Chicago, a man's politics are generally his job.

asks.q: Are you a sailor?
a: Two years on the schooners, from Buffalo to Chicago and Green Bay. Salt, flour, whiskey and settlers out; hides and lead and grain back. The lake is harder than the sea, the old salts say: short steep waves, no room to run, and a lee shore all round.

A November gale off the Manitous that put us on our beam ends for an hour. Two schooners went ashore that night. One of them was never found. Every sailor on these lakes knows a man who went down. We do not talk about them on board.

asks.q: Where did you learn your trade?
a: In the Detroit shipyards, from my uncle, building bateaux and schooners. A boat and a house are not so different: keel and frame, ribs and planks. When the boats stopped needing me, the houses started. Now I build frame houses for Yankees who cannot pronounce my name.

more.q: Do you know the Laframboise family?
a: Everybody does. Charles is a carpenter like me, and his sister Madeleine keeps a boarding house, and Archange makes dresses for the Yankee ladies. Their family has been here since before the fort. Go and ask Charles. He will tell you where the old houses stood.

asks.q: How long have you lived in Chicago?
a: Three years. I came up from Kentucky by way of Indiana, with free papers in my pocket that I show to anybody who asks and some who do not. Illinois is a free state, they say, but it makes a man of my colour post a bond and carry a certificate. Free is a word with a lot of small print.

Better than where I came from, yes. Nobody here can sell me. I have work, I am paid, and there is a man at the barber's and a woman at the laundry who know my name. The first man who ever lived here at this river was a man of colour, they say: Point de Sable, from the Indies. People forget that. I do not.
Some do. The work treats me fairly: a wall I build stands as straight as any other man's. The rest, I keep my own counsel about, and I keep my papers dry.

asks.q: What's that man doing with the chain?
a: Surveying. Every lot in this town has to be measured, staked and written down, and every one of them is being sold three times this summer. The surveyor goes out with his chain and his compass and his boy with the stakes. Half of them are measuring land that is under water half the year.

Accurate enough to start a lawsuit. Every stake is somebody's fortune, and every surveyor's mistake is somebody else's. The old settlers' fences were put where the cows wanted them, and the new lines go where the map says. When the two meet, there is always a fence in somebody's yard.

asks.q: Where's the best whiskey in town?
a: Depends what you want from it. If you want company, the Sauganash, where Mark Beaubien will play the fiddle. If you want it cheap, any shanty by the river. If you want to stay alive, avoid the fellow with one eye down by the landing who sells it out of a barrel he swears is from Kentucky.
River water, raw spirit, a plug of tobacco for the colour and a handful of red pepper for the bite. Men drink it and swear it is the best. In the morning they swear otherwise.

asks.q: Who was here before the boom?
a: The Kinzies, the Beaubiens, the Ouilmettes, the Laframboises, a few soldiers, the traders and their families. A hundred people, perhaps, in thirty-one. Now there are three thousand. The old settlers stand at the corner and watch the new ones arrive like a man watching a flood rise over his field.

The newcomers made them rich, so they cannot complain. But young Kinzie remembers when this was all fields and the Potawatomi camped by the river. Ask him what he thinks of it all. He is too polite to say all of it.

asks.q: Is there a stage coach?
a: There is one to Ottawa and one to Detroit, by way of Niles, when the roads let it go. It is a mud wagon on springs with leather curtains. You sit on a board, you are thrown against the roof at every rut, and when the wheels stick the passengers get out and push.
Only to an enemy. Take a schooner if you are going east. Take a horse if you are going west. Take the stage only if you have no friends and no money and want to lose both.

asks.q: Can a man borrow money here?
a: Easily, and that is the trouble. There is no bank in Chicago yet, but there will be, and meanwhile every merchant gives credit and every land buyer gives notes. A man who owes a thousand dollars and owns lots worth five thousand feels very rich indeed. A man who owes a thousand dollars and owns lots that nobody wants is in trouble.

They are talking about a branch of the State Bank this year. The merchants want it. The Jackson men do not trust banks. Either way, one day this town will have to pay what it owes. I hope I am somewhere else that day.

asks.q: Did you ever cross the old portage?
a: Many times, as a young man, with the fur brigades. From the South Branch up through Mud Lake to the Des Plaines. In spring you paddled most of the way. In summer you waded and pulled and swore. It is the same line where the canal will go, they say. Somebody has finally listened to the voyageurs.

Every trader who ever came this way. Mr. Hubbard did it for years with the American Fur Company before he went into pork. Ask him about the time the boats froze in on the Illinois. He tells it with his hands.

allen_lieut_james.q: What's the biggest problem with the harbour?
a: Sand. The current along this shore carries sand south, and every storm piles it against the north pier and pushes it round the end into the channel. I dredge, I extend the pier, the sand follows. It is a race between the government's money and the lake's patience, and the lake has more of both.

In the end, yes, if Congress keeps paying. A harbour here will make this the greatest port on the lakes. I write that to Washington every month. The major says I write more letters than he does. He is right. Mine have estimates in them.

beaubien_jean_baptiste.q: How long have you been in Chicago?
a: I first came through as a young trader for the Mackinac houses, more than twenty-five years ago, and I have lived here since before the war ended. My first wife was Ottawa, and my second is Josette, whom you may know. Between them I have so many children that I count at supper and still miss one.

She was the Kinzie children's nurse, in the old fort's time, a girl of the Laframboise family. After the war I came back and there she was, grown, with that look she has that tells you she has already decided. Go and see her. She will tell you I proposed. I remember it the other way round.

That on such a day this spring, Jean Baptiste Beaubien entered the land called the Fort Dearborn reservation at the land office of the United States, and paid for it in full. Ninety-four dollars and sixty-one cents. The major says it is worth nothing. Then why is he so angry?

beaubien_josette.q: What do you think of the town now?
a: It is too loud and too fast and full of people who do not say good morning. When I was a girl at the old fort, I knew every face on this river. Now I walk down Lake Street and do not know one in ten. But my children will be rich in it, perhaps, so I do not complain too loudly.

My Laframboise cousins keep boarding houses and make dresses and build houses. Madeleine has a house full of young men who eat like wolves. Go and see her. She is the only person in Chicago who can make a land speculator wash his hands before supper.

beaubien_mark.q: Why did you name your hotel the Sauganash?
a: For Billy Caldwell, my friend, whom the Potawatomi call Sauganash, the Englishman. He is the best-read man in this country and the worst dancer, and he has stayed at my house more nights than he has at his own. When I painted the name on the front, he stood in the mud and read it twice and did not say anything, and then he bought everybody a drink.

The guests sleep three to a bed and two on the floor, and in the morning they come down and eat, and I play them a tune, and they forget about the beds. I have had a governor in my house and a horse thief, sometimes on the same night. Go and ask Billy what he thinks of the name. He will say he is honoured. He means: why not the Caldwell House?

more.q: Will you build a bigger one?
a: Everybody else is building bigger. The Couch brothers have the Tremont with its fine beds. Let them. Nobody ever went to the Tremont for the fiddle.

beaubien_mark.q: Did you really run the ferry?
a: For a while, across the river by my house, in a scow. A few pennies a man and more for a wagon. I would row them over and play them a tune on the other side if they paid double. Now there is the drawbridge and I am a poor man again, which is to say I am exactly as poor as before.

more.q: Is your brother proud of you?
a: My brother the Colonel thinks I should be more serious. I think he should be less. He has the whole fort reservation in a receipt in his pocket and the major breathing on his neck, and I have a fiddle. Ask him which of us sleeps better. I can tell you: it is not him.

caldwell_billy.q: What's it like being a justice of the peace?
a: I marry people, I hear small quarrels about pigs and debts and whose fence is where, and I fine drunks. It is the most American thing that has ever happened to me. A man who rode with Tecumseh, now telling a Yankee he must pay for his neighbour's cabbages.

more.q: Will you go west with your people?
a: I have a reservation here on the North Branch, by the treaty, and I could stay. But I spoke for the bands, and I signed for them, and I think I should go with them, to see that what was promised is given. That is what a man owes the people he spoke for. Go and see Mark at the Sauganash. He has been trying to make me stay with music for a month.

calhoun_john.q: What do you think of the new paper in town?
a: The American? Mr. Davis started it last month and calls it the voice of the people, by which he means the Whigs. Good luck to him. There is room in this town for two papers and fifty opinions. There is not room for two papers' worth of advertisements, and he is learning that already.

We are rivals, which in the newspaper business is better than friends. We drink at the same tavern and we insult each other in print and we borrow each other's type when the boat is late. Go and ask him how his paper supply is holding up. Mine is low. His is lower.

carpenter_philo.q: How many children come to your Sunday school?
a: Forty or fifty, some Sundays, from every kind of family: Yankee, French, Irish, a few Potawatomi from the camps. I teach them their letters from the Bible, and some hymns, and how to sit still for an hour, which is the hardest lesson of all in Chicago.

Mr. Porter, the Presbyterian minister, and his new wife, who was Miss Chappel, the schoolteacher. Between us we have taught half the children of this town to read. Mr. Watkins, the first schoolmaster, sends me his scholars on Sundays. Go and ask him which of them learned their letters from the Bible and which from his charcoal boards.

caton_john_dean.q: What's the most ridiculous case you've had?
a: A man sued his neighbour because the neighbour's pig ate his deed. The deed was in his coat and the coat was on a fence and the pig was hungry. We had to prove the deed existed without the deed. Mr. Hamilton had recorded it, thank God, or the pig would own the lot.

My client got his lot and the neighbour paid for a new coat. The pig was not charged. Go and ask Mr. Hamilton to show you the record. He keeps everything. Even a pig's appetite is a matter of public record in Chicago.

clybourne_archibald.q: What was it like feeding the treaty?
a: Every day for two weeks I killed cattle from dawn and my men cut and carried. Eight thousand people, Potawatomi and Ottawa and Ojibwe, camped all round the town, and the government paid me to feed them while the chiefs and the commissioners talked. I never saw so much meat go so fast, nor so many people in one place.

I saw the tent and the chiefs going in and out, and Caldwell and Robinson walking up and down talking to everybody. When it was signed there was a great deal of noise and then a great quiet. Go and ask Caldwell what it felt like inside the tent. I only know how it felt at the slaughterhouse.

couch_ira.q: How did you build the Tremont?
a: My brother James and I put it up two years ago at Lake and Dearborn: three storeys of frame, painted, with a real dining room and beds with real mattresses. People said it was too grand for Chicago. It has been full every night since the land sale started.

Mark Beaubien at the Sauganash, who has a fiddle where I have a mattress. We send each other our overflow. When I am full, I send them to him, and he plays them to sleep. Go and see him and tell him I have three empty beds tonight. He will laugh. I never do.

Because a town of three thousand with one paper hears only one opinion, and the opinion of the Democrat is that whatever the President does is right. The American is for the canal, for improvement, for a harbour and a railroad, and against men who hold every office and still want more.
We have subscribers and advertisers and enemies, which is everything a paper needs. Mr. Calhoun is a gentleman and a printer and I respect him. Go and tell him I said so. He will not believe you.

dole_george_w.q: What's the secret of a good packing house?
a: Clean salt, tight barrels, cold weather, and buy your cattle before everybody else does. I buy from the drovers who bring them in from the prairie and from Mr. Clybourne up the North Branch. He was supplying the fort before I came. Go and ask him what a steer cost in twenty-nine and what it costs now.

more.q: Will Chicago be a big meat town?
a: The prairie is grass and the grass feeds cattle and the cattle walk here to the lake. Once there is a canal and a railroad, every animal from here to the Mississippi will come through this town. I may not live to see it, but I can see it from here.

egan_william_b.q: Do you treat the Irish workers?
a: I treat everybody, and the Irish come to me because I am one of them. They pay in eggs and promises and sometimes a bottle. A girl came to me last week with her hands so cracked from the washing that they bled. Mary Flynn, a good girl in a lawyer's house. I gave her goose grease and told her to complain. She will not.

more.q: Is it hard being Irish here?
a: For me, a doctor with a good coat, it is a joke at dinner. For the men with the shovels it is no joke. The Yankees want their work and not their company. That will change. There will be too many of us to ignore.

greene_john.q: How many men have you lost to the town?
a: Seven this spring. They go over the pickets at night with their boots in their hands and by morning they are carpenters on Lake Street calling themselves something else. The town hides them. A carpenter is worth more to Chicago than a private is to me.

more.q: What will happen to the fort?
a: The War Department will close it, I expect, and soon. It guards nothing but itself now. When it goes, Lieutenant Allen's harbour will be the only thing the army has here. Go and talk to him. His work will last. Mine will be a story.

hamilton_richard_j.q: How do you do six jobs at once?
a: By writing very fast and never sleeping. In the morning I record deeds, at noon I hear probate, in the afternoon I am school commissioner, in the evening I am the county clerk. I have one desk and I change hats. Sometimes I forget which hat I have on and sell a school lot to a dead man.

more.q: Who brings you the most work?
a: The lawyers, and young Caton most of all. He brings me deeds with three owners and wills with no witnesses and smiles as if it were a gift. Go and see him. He owes me a dinner.

hogan_john_s_c.q: What's the strangest letter you've had?
a: A letter addressed To My Son, Chicago, Illinois, in an old woman's hand from Ireland, with no name at all. I put it in the window with a note. Four men came to claim it. None of them could say what was in it. In the end a young Irishman named Mahoney read the first line over my shoulder and started to cry, and I gave it to him.

I believe so. He said nobody else's mother called her son a gom. Go and ask him. He may tell you what she said. He may tell you she sent a holy medal, which I am sure she did not, because I felt the envelope.

Pork, in barrels, salted and packed for the boats east. Hides. Some furs still. Flour. Salt from Syracuse. Whatever the town needs and whatever the country sends. I built the first brick building of any size in Chicago for it, and they laughed at me. They are not laughing now.

George Dole packed the first barrels out of here in thirty-two and showed it could be done. I packed hogs on a bigger scale, and they called my warehouse Hubbard's Folly because nobody could imagine so many hogs. Go and ask Dole what he thinks of my hogs. He will say mine are fatter. He is being kind.

Nobody knows, though everybody has a theory. Bad air off the marshes, the doctors say: miasma. The old settlers say it is the new ground being broken, the smell of the turned earth. The Potawatomi say it is the season. All I know is quinine helps, and that it comes worst in late summer when the sloughs go low.

more.q: Do you and Dr. Egan agree?
a: We agree about nothing except the price of quinine, which is too high. He thinks I am too cautious and I think he is too cheerful. Go and ask him. He will make a speech about it and sing a song at the end.

kinzie_john_h.q: What does an Indian agent do?
a: I was the government's agent at Fort Winnebago for the Winnebago nation: hand out the annuity money and goods, settle quarrels, keep the peace, write a great many reports. Now I am here in Chicago, in business, and helping where I can with the payment and the removal of the Potawatomi.

I have known these people all my life. I sat in a boat with my nurse at the river mouth in the summer of 1812 while a Potawatomi chief stood guard over us. I will not tell you the treaty is fair. I will tell you it was the best that men like Caldwell could get from a government that wanted all of it. Go and ask him. He will be more honest than I can afford to be.
I miss the quiet. I do not miss the winters. My wife says the quiet was worth it. She wrote everything down there. She says one day she will make a book of it.

Everyone who matters and some who think they do. The officers from the fort, the doctors, Mr. Hubbard, the Beaubiens, any traveller with a letter of introduction, and once a missionary who stayed six weeks. I give them venison and whitefish and wild rice and whatever came on the last boat. And I make them sing.

Voyageur songs, in French, with his eyes shut, because he learned them in the canoes when he was sixteen. Then he tells the story of the ride to Danville and every time the miles get longer. Go and ask him how far it was. Then ask me afterwards.

kinzie_juliette.q: What did your husband's mother tell you?
a: Everything about the old fort and the summer of 1812: the council, the medal, the boat, the chiefs who protected the family. She made me promise to write it down one day, all of it, so it would not be lost. I have been taking notes ever since. Some of what she said I can hardly bear to write.

Josette Beaubien was the children's nurse in that boat. She remembers more than she says. Go and ask her, gently. She will tell you about the morning on the water. She will not tell you about the afternoon.

newberry_walter_loomis.q: Why buy land where there's nothing?
a: Because there will be something. The town is crowded on the south side by the fort and the river, and it has nowhere to go but north and west. Kinzie's addition on the north bank is already being sold off. My acres are beyond that, out on the prairie. In ten years they will be streets.

Then I will have a very large farm. A man who buys at a few dollars an acre can afford to be wrong. The men buying on Lake Street at two thousand a lot cannot. Go and ask young Kinzie. His father's land on the north side is being cut into lots this summer, and he knows what it was.

I came for a month and I have stayed a month and I am beginning to think I will stay longer. I sold a third of my brother-in-law's land last week for more than he paid for the whole. The rest I am holding. I wrote to him: send me more land.

more.q: What does the town need most?
a: A railroad, a canal, a drained street and an honest county record. Mr. Hamilton keeps the records, and he is honest, and he has six jobs. Go and see him. Ask him how many deeds he recorded today. Then ask him if he has eaten.

peck_philip.q: What was Chicago like when you came?
a: Four years ago it was the fort, a few dozen log houses, some French families, and a great deal of nothing. My store was the first frame building on South Water Street and people walked out to look at it. Now I cannot see it for the buildings round it.

Otis Bardwell and his horses, mostly. He is the best teamster in town and he will tell you so. His horses are better than most men's children. Go and ask him their names. You will hear about them for an hour.

rc_bardwell_otis.q: What makes Dan and Duke so special?
a: They are matched bays out of Kentucky, sixteen hands, and they pull together like one horse. Dan is the thinker; he looks at a mud hole and goes round it. Duke is the strong one; he goes through it. Between them they have never left a load behind, except the bricks, and that was the road's fault.

more.q: Is it true about the hay wagon?
a: I was the man driving it. I did not notice a thing. A man fell two storeys into my hay and I drove him half a mile before he climbed out and thanked me. That is Patrick Mahoney. Go and ask him for the rest. Tell him I want a share of his luck.

One on the harbour, driving piles for Lieutenant Allen. One gone to the lead mines at Galena. The youngest, God help him, buying and selling lots like a Yankee, with money he does not have. I see the eldest at Mass on Sundays. The others I hear about.

Everybody knows Patrick Mahoney. He is the luckiest man in Chicago and the worst at keeping his money. He fell off a roof into a hay wagon and found a dollar in the mud the same week. Go and ask him to tell it. He tells it better every time, and I correct him.

rc_mahoney_patrick.q: Can I see your lucky medal?
a: Here it is, round my neck, the Blessed Virgin, a bit worn from my thumb. My mother gave it to me on the quay at Cork. I have touched it every morning since. I touched it before I fell off that roof, and look what happened. Landed soft as a baby.

She did, and the letter found me, which is a miracle in itself. Mr. Hogan at the post office will tell you how. She said I was a gom and to keep away from roofs. I have not been on one since. Go and thank Mr. Hogan for me. I never did it properly.

robinson_alexander.q: How did you get the wounded captain to Mackinac?
a: In a canoe, my wife and I, after the battle in 1812, with Captain Heald wounded and his wife wounded worse, up the whole length of the lake, three hundred miles. We paddled in the day and hid at night. The British commandant at Mackinac took them in. They lived. I was paid in thanks.

Because they were alive and somebody had to. I was a trader; I knew the Healds; it was a canoe and a lake. Afterwards some people on both sides said I should have done otherwise. Young Kinzie remembers those days. Go and ask him who else helped. There were more of us than the stories say.

st_cyr_john_mary.q: How did St. Mary's come to be built?
a: The French Catholics of this town wrote to the Bishop at St. Louis two years ago asking for a priest, and the Bishop sent me. We built a little frame church, twenty-five feet by thirty-five, by the river, for four hundred dollars. The Beaubiens gave most of the money and the Irish gave their backs.

The French, the Irish, a few Germans, some Potawatomi, and the occasional Yankee who has lost a bet. I say the Mass in Latin, preach in French and English, and hear confession in four languages, badly in two of them. Go and thank Colonel Beaubien for me. He has never let me want for wood in winter.

watkins_john.q: What became of your first pupils?
a: Some are clerks now, some are married, some have gone west with their families. One of the Beaubien boys keeps the books in a store now, if you can imagine it. Mark Beaubien sent three of his children to me, and every one of them could play the fiddle better than he could read.

A little. There are more teachers now, and a real school house is promised. I am glad to be the first and gladder not to be the only. Go and ask Mark what he thinks of schooling. He will tell you a fiddle never failed him.
